name: CDS
tagline: Become a commissioned officer after graduation through IMA, INA, AFA or OTA.

overview.about: The Combined Defence Services Examination is held by UPSC twice a year for graduates. It leads to the Indian Military Academy (Dehradun), Indian Naval Academy (Ezhimala), Air Force Academy (Dundigal, Hyderabad) and Officers' Training Academy (Chennai, Short Service Commission). Written qualifiers face the SSB interview (300 marks for IMA/INA/AFA, 200 for OTA) and medicals.

IMA, INA and AFA: unmarried men; OTA: men and women (as per the notification). Final-year students may apply provisionally

cards.title: CDS English at a glance
cards.body: English is 100 marks in 2 hours and is compulsory for every academy, including OTA. It is also used as a qualifying screen — a weak English score can cost you even if your GK is good. Areas: spotting errors, sentence improvement, fill-in-the-blanks, synonyms, antonyms, idioms, ordering and comprehension.

cards.title: Pronouns and comparisons
cards.body: A pronoun must agree with its noun in number and gender. In comparisons, compare like with like: 'The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi' (not 'than Delhi'). Use 'between' for two, 'among' for more than two.

cards.title: Common confusions
cards.body: Less (uncountable) vs fewer (countable): 'fewer cadets', 'less water'. 'Lay' needs an object; 'lie' does not. 'Hardly/scarcely… when' and 'no sooner… than' are fixed pairs. Avoid double negatives like 'hardly never'.

cards.title: Conditionals and tense sequence
cards.body: First conditional: If + present, will + verb ('If it rains, we will stay'). Second: If + past, would + verb. Third: If + had + V3, would have + V3. A past-tense main verb usually takes a past-tense reported clause ('He said that he **was** tired').

cards.title: Sentence improvement
cards.body: 'No sooner had the bell rang when the cadets ran out.' Two errors: 'rang' should be 'rung' (past participle after 'had'), and 'no sooner' pairs with 'than'. Correct: **'No sooner had the bell rung than the cadets ran out.'**

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Keep a personal 'error log'. Every wrong answer in a mock goes into the log with the rule behind it. Re-read the log before each mock — the same 30–40 rules cover most CDS error questions.

cards.q: Choose the correct sentence:
options: There were less cadets on parade today.
There were fewer cadets on parade today.
There were lesser cadets on parade today.
There was fewer cadets on parade today.
cards.explain: 'Cadets' are countable, so use 'fewer', with the plural verb 'were'.

cards.q: Fill in the blank: 'No sooner did he arrive ___ it started raining.'
Choose the correct option: 'If I ___ you, I would accept the offer.'
cards.explain: In the second (hypothetical) conditional, formal English uses 'were' for all persons.

notes.h: What CDS grammar questions look like
notes.p:
The CDS English paper has **120 questions in 2 hours**, and grammar appears as **spotting errors**, **sentence improvement** and grammar-based **fill in the blanks**. Each wrong answer costs one-third of the question's marks, so accuracy matters more than attempting everything.

The fastest method is a fixed checklist. For every sentence, test: (1) subject–verb agreement, (2) tense consistency, (3) pronoun case and reference, (4) articles, (5) prepositions, (6) adjectives and adverbs, (7) conjunction pairs, (8) parallel structure. With practice the error usually jumps out at step 1 or 2.

**Agreement:** collective nouns (team, jury, committee) take a singular verb when acting as one unit and a plural verb when members act individually: "The jury **was** unanimous" vs "The jury **were** divided in their opinions." Words like "news", "mathematics", "physics" and "politics" (as a subject of study) are singular.

**Tense sequence:** a past tense in the main clause is usually followed by a past tense in the reported clause: "He said that he **was** tired." Universal truths stay in the present: "The teacher said that the Earth **revolves** round the Sun."

**Conditionals:**
points: Type 1 (likely): If you **work** hard, you **will** pass
Type 2 (imaginary present): If I **were** rich, I **would** help them
Type 3 (past, impossible now): If he **had left** early, he **would have caught** the train
Never use 'would' in the if-clause: 'If he would have come' is wrong

notes.p: CDS options often contain a word that is almost right. Learn these pairs:
points: Fewer (countable: fewer soldiers) vs less (uncountable: less water)
Each other (two) vs one another (more than two) — modern usage is relaxed, but exams follow the rule
Lie (rest; lay, lain) vs lay (put; laid, laid)
Beside (next to) vs besides (in addition to)
Scarcely/hardly … when; no sooner … than; not only … but also; either … or; neither … nor
'Lest' is followed by 'should': work hard lest you should fail

notes.p:
**Example 1.** "The furniture in the officers' mess (a) / are made of (b) / seasoned teak. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(b)**. "Furniture" is uncountable and singular → "is made of".

**Example 2.** "No sooner did the whistle blow (a) / when the cadets (b) / started running. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(b)**. "No sooner" pairs with "than", not "when".

**Example 3.** "One of my friends (a) / have joined (b) / the Indian Navy. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(b)**. The subject is "one" → "has joined".

**Example 4 (improvement).** "He is **one of the best players that has** represented the country."
Answer: "that **have**". The relative pronoun refers to "players" (plural), so the verb is plural.

Read the whole sentence before looking at the parts — errors often sit in the part you'd skim. If the sentence sounds fine, check the less obvious rules: articles before abbreviations ("an NCC cadet"), adverb placement ("He **only** scored ten runs" vs "He scored **only** ten runs"), and superfluous words ("return back", "repeat again", "discuss about").

Practice tip: solve 20 error-spotting questions daily from previous years' CDS papers, and write the rule next to every mistake you make. Within a month your personal "error list" will show the 4–5 rules you keep forgetting.
Glance at these before every English mock.
points: Check the true subject; 'one of' takes a singular verb
Furniture, information, advice, luggage — uncountable, singular
Universal truths stay in the present tense
Fewer for countable, less for uncountable
Cut redundant words: return back, discuss about

cards.title: Three question types, one method
cards.body: Synonyms, antonyms and one-word substitutions all test meaning. Read every option before marking — UPSC often places a close-but-wrong option first. If unsure, think of the word in a sentence you know.

cards.title: Idioms worth knowing
points: Blessing in disguise — something good that first seemed bad
Beat around the bush — avoid the main point
Bite the bullet — face something difficult bravely
At the eleventh hour — at the last moment
Hold your horses — be patient, wait

cards.title: One-word substitutions
points: Bilingual — one who speaks two languages
Atheist — one who does not believe in God
Mercenary — a soldier hired to fight for a foreign country

cards.title: Learn words by roots
cards.body: Prefixes change meaning predictably: 'in-/im-/un-' (not), 'pre-' (before), 'post-' (after), 'omni-' (all). Roots: 'bell' = war (belligerent), 'loqu' = speak (eloquent), 'fid' = faith (confident, infidel). One root unlocks a family of words.

cards.title: Eliminating options
cards.body: Antonym of 'Belligerent': (a) hostile (b) aggressive (c) peaceable (d) quarrelsome. 'Bell' means war, so belligerent = warlike. (a), (b), (d) are synonyms. The antonym is **peaceable**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Spend 15 minutes daily on vocabulary with spaced revision (day 1, 3, 7, 30). Quality beats quantity — 10 words revised properly each day is better than 50 read once.

cards.q: 'At the eleventh hour' means:
cards.explain: The idiom means at the latest possible moment.

cards.q: One word for 'a soldier hired to serve in a foreign army':

cards.q: Choose the antonym of 'Belligerent':

notes.h: Why vocabulary carries so many marks
notes.p:
In CDS English, vocabulary appears in **synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases**, and indirectly in comprehension and cloze. Together these can be a large share of the paper, and each question takes only seconds if you know the word — making this the highest-return area for revision.

Learn words actively: write the word, its meaning, a synonym, an antonym and one sentence of your own. Revise using spaced repetition — the next day, after a week, and after a month.
These are asked almost every year. Group them by theme so they stick:
points: People: philanthropist (loves mankind), misanthrope (hates mankind), misogynist (hates women), polyglot (speaks many languages), altruist (selfless), egoist (self-centred)
Fear and belief: atheist (does not believe in God), agnostic (says God's existence cannot be known), hydrophobia (fear of water), claustrophobia (fear of closed spaces)
Death and writing: posthumous (after death), epitaph (words on a tomb), obituary (notice of death), autobiography (life written by oneself)
Government: autocracy (rule by one), bureaucracy (rule by officials), anarchy (absence of government), plutocracy (rule by the rich)
Others: panacea (cure for all ills), insolvent (unable to pay debts), infallible (cannot make mistakes), inaudible (cannot be heard), illegible (cannot be read)

notes.p: Idioms are tested by asking for the meaning of a phrase in a sentence. Never translate literally; think of the situation in which it is used.
points: At the eleventh hour — at the last possible moment
To take the bull by the horns — to face a difficulty boldly
A wild goose chase — a hopeless or pointless search
To call a spade a spade — to speak plainly
To smell a rat — to suspect something wrong
In the doldrums — in low spirits, inactive
To bite the dust — to be defeated or to die
To leave no stone unturned — to make every possible effort
To be on the horns of a dilemma — to face two equally difficult choices

notes.p:
**Step 1:** decide whether the word is positive, negative or neutral. **Step 2:** remove options of the wrong tone. **Step 3:** among the rest, pick the closest meaning in the same part of speech. **Step 4:** in antonym questions, cross out the option that is a synonym — examiners deliberately include one.

**Example 1.** Synonym of "obstinate": (a) stubborn (b) obedient (c) humble (d) cowardly. Answer: **(a) stubborn**.

**Example 2.** Antonym of "ephemeral": (a) temporary (b) brief (c) eternal (d) fragile. "Ephemeral" means short-lived; (a) and (b) are synonyms. Answer: **(c) eternal**.

**Example 3.** Antonym of "affluent": (a) wealthy (b) impoverished (c) generous (d) proud. Answer: **(b) impoverished**.

notes.h: Roots that unlock hundreds of words
notes.p: A small set of Latin and Greek roots explains a large part of exam vocabulary: **bene** (good) — benevolent; **mal** (bad) — malevolent; **voc** (call) — vocal, advocate; **dict** (say) — predict, contradict; **ver** (truth) — verify, veracity; **cred** (believe) — credible, incredulous; **ambi** (both) — ambiguous, ambivalent; **pseudo** (false) — pseudonym. When you meet an unknown word in the exam, break it into parts — it often gives enough of a clue to eliminate options.
Test yourself: cover the meanings and say them aloud.
points: Write every new word in a sentence of your own
Idioms: eleventh hour, smell a rat, Achilles' heel
Antonym questions hide a synonym among the options
Use roots to guess unfamiliar words

cards.title: Reading comprehension
cards.body: CDS passages are usually short and opinion-based. Read the questions first, then read the passage actively — note the author's main point and tone. Mark answers only from what is written or clearly implied.

cards.title: Tone and inference
cards.body: Tone words: critical, optimistic, sarcastic, neutral, analytical. Inference means a conclusion the passage supports without stating it outright. Reject options that are too extreme ('always', 'never') or bring in outside information.

cards.title: Cloze test
cards.body: Read the whole passage once before filling any blank. Fill the easy blanks first; they reveal the context for the hard ones. Check collocations: 'pay attention', 'take responsibility', 'make a decision'.

cards.title: Sentence ordering (S1, P, Q, R, S6)
cards.body: When the first and last sentences are given, the middle ones must connect them logically. Look for pronoun links ('he', 'this'), connectors ('but', 'therefore') and general-to-specific flow. Fix one pair, then check which options contain it.

cards.title: Using a mandatory pair
cards.body: If sentence Q says 'This decision…' and only sentence P mentions a decision, then P must come right before Q. Any option without 'PQ' together can be eliminated immediately — often leaving only one answer.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Comprehension and ordering take time. Attempt vocabulary and error questions first, then return to passages with the remaining time. Never leave the paper without reading at least one passage — they are high-accuracy marks.

cards.q: In comprehension, an 'inference' is:
options: A fact stated word for word
A conclusion supported by the passage but not stated directly
cards.explain: Inference questions test what the passage logically implies.

cards.q: Which word best completes: 'Cadets must pay ___ to every instruction.'

notes.h: Reading comprehension: the biggest single block
notes.p:
Comprehension passages usually carry several questions each, so they deserve a fixed method. Read the questions first (just the stems, not the options) so you know what to look for. Then read the passage at a steady pace, noting in two or three words what each paragraph says.

Question types and how to handle them:
points: Factual: the answer is stated directly — locate the line and match it
Inference: the answer is implied — choose the option that must be true, not one that might be true
Main idea / title: choose the option that covers the whole passage
Author's tone: positive, critical, neutral, ironic, etc. — look at adjectives the author uses
Vocabulary in context: the meaning in this passage may differ from the common meaning

notes.p:
Wrong options are designed to look attractive. Watch for: options that are **true in real life but not stated** in the passage; options with **extreme words** (always, never, completely, only); options that are **too narrow** (one detail) for a main-idea question; and options that **reverse** the passage's cause and effect.

**Example.** A passage says: "Regular exercise improves concentration in many students." Which can be inferred? (a) All students who exercise concentrate better. (b) Exercise can help students focus. Option (a) uses "all" — too extreme. Answer: **(b)**.

Read the full passage once without filling anything. Then fill each blank by checking **grammar** (tense, singular/plural, part of speech), **collocation** (words that naturally go together, like "take a decision", "pay attention", "commit a crime") and **logic** (connectors like however, therefore, despite signal contrast or result).

**Example.** "The patrol was exhausted; ___, it pressed on to reach the post before dark." Options: therefore / however / because / moreover. The second part contrasts with exhaustion, so the answer is **however**.
In ordering questions, the first and last sentences are sometimes fixed and you arrange the middle parts, or you arrange all parts of a jumbled sentence or paragraph. A step-by-step approach:
points: Find the opening: it introduces a subject with a full name or idea, not a pronoun like 'he' or 'this'
Find mandatory pairs: a pronoun must follow the noun it refers to ('the general… he')
Use connectors: 'however', 'as a result', 'then', 'finally' show sequence
Use time order: earlier events come before later ones
Check the options: once you fix one pair, eliminate options that break it — you rarely need the full order

notes.p:
Parts of a sentence: "The young officer (P) / despite heavy rain (Q) / led his platoon (R) / across the swollen river (S)."

Step 1: The subject "The young officer" must open the sentence → P first.
Step 2: The verb "led his platoon" naturally follows the subject → R.
Step 3: "across the swollen river" completes the action → S.
Step 4: "despite heavy rain" can close the sentence → Q.
Answer: **PRSQ** — "The young officer led his platoon across the swollen river despite heavy rain." Look for that option; if PQRS is also offered, check which reads more naturally.
Use this checklist in every mock.
points: Read question stems first, then the passage
Answer from the passage, not from your own knowledge
Ordering: find the opener, then pronoun–noun pairs and connectors
Eliminate options once one pair is fixed
Practise one passage and one ordering set daily

cards.title: The task
cards.body: A sentence has a **bold or underlined part**. You choose the option that improves it, or "No improvement". Read the whole sentence; the error is usually agreement, tense, preposition, comparison or a wrong word.

cards.title: High-yield rules
points: "One of the + plural noun + singular verb" (One of the boys is…)

cards.title: Tense sequence
cards.body: A past tense in the main clause usually takes a past tense in the subordinate clause: He said that he **was** tired. Universal truths stay in the present: He said that the earth **revolves** round the sun.

cards.title: Example
cards.body: "If I was you, I would accept." Improvement: **If I were you** — the subjunctive for unreal conditions.

cards.title: Example
cards.body: "He is senior than me." Improvement: **senior to me**. Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) take "to".

cards.title: Method
cards.body: Read the sentence; predict the correction; then scan options. If two options are grammatically fine, prefer the shorter, more idiomatic one. Pick "No improvement" only after checking agreement, tense and prepositions.

cards.q: Improve: "Hardly had he reached the station than the train left."
Improve: "Unless you do not work hard, you will fail."
options: If you do not work hard
Until you do not work hard
cards.explain: "Unless" already means "if not", so "unless … not" is a double negative.

cards.q: Improve: "Neither the captain nor the players was present."
cards.explain: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "players" (plural).

notes.p:
Sentence improvement is one of the regular question types in the CDS English paper, alongside spotting errors, ordering, synonyms, antonyms, fill in the blanks, cloze and comprehension (the mix varies by paper). The official syllabus only says the paper tests "understanding of English and workmanlike use of words", so grammar is tested through usage rather than rules.

Each item checks one idea. Identify **which rule** is being tested before you look at options; options are designed so that a vague "sounds fine" approach picks a wrong one.

**Example 1.** "The quality of the mangoes were not good."
Step 1: Subject is "quality" (singular), not "mangoes".
Step 2: Correction: **was not good**.

**Example 2.** "Bread and butter are my favourite breakfast."
Step 1: "Bread and butter" is a single dish.
Step 2: Correction: **is my favourite breakfast**.

With "as well as", "along with", "together with", the verb agrees with the first subject: The teacher, along with the students, **was** present.

Type 1: If + present, will + base (If it rains, I will stay). Type 2: If + past, would + base (If I were rich, I would travel). Type 3: If + past perfect, would have + past participle (If he had studied, he would have passed).

**Example 3.** "If he would have come, I would have met him." Correction: **If he had come**. Never use "would" in the if-clause.

The present perfect cannot take a definite past time: "I have seen him yesterday" → **I saw him yesterday**. "Since" takes a point of time and "for" a period: since Monday, for three days.

Fixed pairs: **comply with**, **abide by**, **consist of**, **senior to**, **prefer to**, **married to**, **accused of**, **charged with**, **superior to**. Comparisons must compare like with like: "The climate of Shimla is better than **that of** Delhi."

Redundancy errors: "return back", "repeat again", "cousin brother", "the reason is because" — remove the extra word. **Example 4.** "He returned back home." → **returned home**.

**Example 5.** "Each of the soldiers have been given a medal." Subject "each" is singular → **has been given**.

Do not change the meaning of the sentence while fixing it. Watch for options that fix one error and introduce another. Questions also test confusables: **lie/lay**, **beside/besides**, **loose/lose**, **affect/effect**, **economic/economical**. With negative marking, skip only when two options remain and neither can be eliminated.
Rules that recur.
points: One of + plural noun + singular verb
Neither/either…nor/or: verb agrees with the nearer subject

cards.title: How they are asked
cards.body: A word appears in a sentence and you choose the closest (synonym) or most opposite (antonym) meaning. The **context** fixes the sense when a word has several meanings.

cards.title: Elimination method
cards.body: 1) Decide whether the word is positive or negative. 2) Cut options of the wrong tone. 3) For antonyms, beware of synonyms planted as options — and vice versa. 4) Check that your choice fits the sentence.

cards.title: Synonym
cards.body: "His **candid** remarks surprised everyone." Candid = **frank**, open, honest.

cards.title: Antonym
cards.body: "The minister's speech was **verbose**." Verbose = wordy; antonym = **concise** (or terse, laconic).

cards.title: Build lists
cards.body: Learn words in pairs (ameliorate/aggravate, frugal/extravagant, ephemeral/permanent, gregarious/reclusive). Pairs double your coverage for both question types.

cards.q: Synonym of "ephemeral":
cards.explain: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time.

cards.q: Antonym of "frugal":
cards.explain: Frugal = thrifty; its opposite is extravagant.

cards.q: Synonym of "obstinate":
cards.explain: Obstinate means stubbornly refusing to change.

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus states that the English paper tests "**workmanlike use of words**". Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions and idioms together usually make up a large share of the paper, and these are quick marks if your vocabulary is solid.

Two habits build vocabulary: reading an English newspaper editorial daily and keeping a notebook of new words with a sentence each.
points: Learn words in context, not isolation
Use roots and affixes to guess unknown words

notes.p:
**Example 1.** "The general was known for his **sagacity**." Options: (a) bravery (b) wisdom (c) cruelty (d) wealth.
Step 1: "Sage" means a wise person — a root clue.
Step 2: The tone is positive; cruelty is out.
Step 3: Bravery is positive but different. Answer **wisdom**.

**Example 2.** "The witness gave a **lucid** account." Lucid = clear, easily understood. Options like "lengthy" or "lucky" are sound-alike traps.

**Example 3.** Antonym of "**garrulous**": (a) talkative (b) taciturn (c) cheerful (d) angry.
Step 1: Garrulous = excessively talkative.
Step 2: (a) is a synonym planted as a trap.
Step 3: Answer **taciturn** (habitually silent).

Prefixes create many antonyms directly: legible/illegible, possible/impossible, regular/irregular, mature/immature, but note that **inflammable** means the same as flammable — not its opposite.

**Example 4.** Antonym of "**ameliorate**": (a) improve (b) worsen (c) relieve (d) restore.
Step 1: Ameliorate = make something bad better.
Step 2: (a), (c) and (d) all move towards "better" and are traps.
Step 3: Answer **worsen** (aggravate).

Word → meaning → opposite:
• **Abundant** (plentiful) ↔ scarce
• **Benevolent** (kind) ↔ malevolent
• **Candid** (frank) ↔ evasive
• **Diligent** (hard-working) ↔ indolent
• **Ephemeral** (short-lived) ↔ perpetual
• **Frugal** (thrifty) ↔ extravagant
• **Gregarious** (sociable) ↔ reclusive
• **Haughty** (proud) ↔ humble
• **Lethargic** (sluggish) ↔ energetic
• **Meticulous** (careful) ↔ careless
• **Obstinate** (stubborn) ↔ docile
• **Prudent** (wise) ↔ rash

Some questions test correct usage: **principal** (main) vs **principle** (rule); **stationary** (still) vs **stationery** (paper); **complement** (complete) vs **compliment** (praise); **eminent** (famous) vs **imminent** (about to happen); **credible** (believable) vs **creditable** (praiseworthy). Learn these as pairs with one example sentence each.

A quick weekly routine works well: on day 1 learn 20 new words with sentences; on day 3 test yourself on meanings; on day 7 test yourself on opposites of the same words. Words you miss go into the next week's list. Over a few months this covers most words that recur in defence-exam papers.
Vocabulary habits.
points: Decide tone first: positive or negative
Watch for planted synonyms in antonym questions
Use roots: bene, mal, loqu, chron, omni

chapters.title: English: fill in the blanks — prepositions, articles & words

cards.title: Types of blanks
cards.body: Blanks test **prepositions**, **articles**, **verb forms**, **conjunctions** or **vocabulary**. Read the whole sentence first — the clue is often after the blank.

cards.title: Articles
points: "a" before consonant sounds: a university, a one-rupee coin
"an" before vowel sounds: an hour, an MLA, an honest man
"the" with unique things, superlatives, rivers, oceans, mountain ranges
No article with names of single mountains, lakes, or most countries

cards.title: Prepositions of time and place
points: at + exact time; on + day/date; in + month/year
in + large place; at + specific point
between two; among more than two
since + point of time; for + duration

cards.title: Fixed prepositions
points: afraid of, fond of, capable of
good at, angry with (person), angry at (thing)
interested in, confident of, accustomed to
differ from, independent of, sensitive to

cards.title: Example
cards.body: "He has been living here ___ 2019." Since marks a point in time → **since**.

cards.title: Vocabulary blanks
cards.body: Look for **signal words**: "although/but" signal contrast; "and/moreover" signal continuation; "because/so" signal cause and effect. Choose the word that fits the signal.

cards.q: She is ___ honest woman.
cards.explain: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound (silent h).

cards.q: The prize was divided ___ the three winners.
cards.explain: "Among" is used for more than two.

cards.q: Although he was rich, he lived a ___ life.

notes.p:
Fill-in-the-blank questions, alone or as a cloze passage, test whether you know which word naturally fits. Read the full sentence, identify the **grammatical slot** (noun, verb, preposition, article) and the **meaning clue**, then choose.

Most errors come from reading only up to the blank. The words after it usually decide the answer: "He was accused ___ theft" needs **of** because of the verb "accused".
points: Identify the part of speech needed
Check the whole sentence with your choice

notes.p:
"A" and "an" depend on **sound**, not spelling: **a** European, **a** uniform, **an** hour, **an** FIR. "The" is used for things already mentioned or unique (the sun, the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Indian Ocean), with superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first) and before a singular noun representing a class (The tiger is a wild animal).

**Example 1.** "___ Ganga is ___ holy river."
Step 1: Rivers take "the".
Step 2: "holy" starts with a consonant sound.
Answer: **The**, **a**.

**Example 2.** "The train will arrive ___ 6 p.m. ___ Monday."
Step 1: Exact clock time → at.
Step 2: Day → on.
Answer: **at**, **on**.

**Example 3.** "She is good ___ mathematics but weak ___ English." Answer: **at**, **in**.

Other fixed uses: **die of** a disease, **die from** a wound; **agree with** a person, **agree to** a proposal; **wait for** someone; **look forward to** + -ing (I look forward to meeting you).

Blanks often test tense sequence: "By the time we reached, the film ___ (start)" → **had started** (past perfect for the earlier action). Conjunctions must fit the logic: "He was tired, ___ he kept working" → **yet**/**but**. "Not only … but also" and "either … or" are fixed pairs.

**Example 4.** "If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be cancelled." Options: rains / will rain / rained / would rain.
Step 1: Main clause is "will be cancelled" → a Type 1 conditional.
Step 2: The if-clause takes the simple present.
Answer: **rains**.

Choosing "an" before words like "university" or "one" (they start with a consonant sound); using "between" for more than two items; and choosing a word with the right meaning but the wrong collocation (we "make a mistake", not "do a mistake"; we "pay attention", not "give attention").

In a cloze passage, read the full paragraph once before filling any blank — the theme and tone of the passage decide vocabulary choices, and a word chosen early may be contradicted by a later sentence.
Rules for blanks.
points: at time, on day, in month/year

cards.title: Socio-religious reformers
cards.body: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the **Brahmo Samaj** (1828) and campaigned against sati. Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the **Arya Samaj** (1875). Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Jyotiba Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873).

cards.title: Governors-General and Viceroys
points: Warren Hastings: first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act, 1773)
Lord William Bentinck: first Governor-General of India (Charter Act, 1833); abolished sati (1829)

cards.title: Bhakti and Sufi movements
cards.body: Medieval saints preached devotion over ritual. Bhakti: Ramanuja, Kabir, Guru Nanak (founder of Sikhism), Mirabai, Tulsidas, Chaitanya. Sufi: Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi). Both stressed love, equality and simple faith.

cards.title: Congress sessions to remember
points: 1907 Surat: split into Moderates and Extremists

cards.title: Towards independence
cards.body: The Cripps Mission (1942) failed; Quit India followed in August 1942. The Cabinet Mission (1946) proposed a Constituent Assembly. The Mountbatten Plan (June 1947) led to Partition and the Indian Independence Act, 1947.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: CDS history questions often ask 'who founded what' and 'arrange in chronological order'. A single timeline sheet from 1757 to 1947 is your most valuable revision tool.

cards.q: Who was the first Viceroy of India?
cards.explain: After the 1858 Act, Lord Canning became the first Viceroy.

cards.q: The Arya Samaj was founded by:
cards.explain: Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 in Bombay.

cards.q: The Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at which Congress session?
cards.explain: The Lahore session of December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, declared complete independence as the goal.

notes.p: CDS history questions range from ancient India to the national movement, with the **modern period usually getting the most weight**. Questions are often statement-based ("Which of the statements given above is/are correct?") or matching-type, so you need precise facts, not just stories. Use NCERT history books (old and new) as your base and make short tables of pairs — person, event, year.
Revise these high-yield pairs:
points: Harappan sites: Lothal (dockyard), Kalibangan (ploughed field), Mohenjo-daro (Great Bath), Dholavira (water management)
Arthashastra — Kautilya; Indica — Megasthenes; Harshacharita — Banabhatta
Ashoka's edicts were first deciphered by James Prinsep
Nalanda flourished under the Guptas and Harsha; Hiuen Tsang studied there
Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526): Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi
Mughal administration: mansabdari (Akbar); Sher Shah introduced the rupiya

notes.p: Matching questions often pair an official with a reform:
points: Warren Hastings — first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773)
Lord Cornwallis — Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793)
Lord William Bentinck — first Governor-General of India (Charter Act 1833); abolished sati (1829)
Lord Dalhousie — Doctrine of Lapse; first railway line Bombay–Thane (1853); telegraph
Lord Ripon — local self-government (1882); Ilbert Bill controversy
Lord Mountbatten — last Viceroy; C. Rajagopalachari — only Indian Governor-General

notes.p:
The 19th-century reform movements are a CDS favourite. **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** founded the **Brahmo Samaj** (1828) and campaigned against sati. **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** championed widow remarriage, legalised by the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856. **Swami Dayananda Saraswati** founded the **Arya Samaj** (1875) with the call "Back to the Vedas". **Jyotiba Phule** founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj** (1873) and, with Savitribai Phule, opened schools for girls. **Swami Vivekananda** founded the **Ramakrishna Mission** (1897). **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (1875).

Newspapers: **Kesari** — Bal Gangadhar Tilak; **Young India** and **Harijan** — Gandhi; **Al-Hilal** — Maulana Abul Kalam Azad; **Hicky's Bengal Gazette** (1780) — India's first newspaper.
Memorise this backbone and attach details to it:
points: 1885 INC founded → 1905 Partition of Bengal → 1906 Muslim League → 1907 Surat split
1916 Lucknow Pact and Home Rule Leagues (Tilak, Annie Besant)
1919 Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh (13 April) → 1920 Non-Cooperation → 1922 Chauri Chaura
1928 Simon Commission → 1929 Lahore session, Purna Swaraj
1930 Dandi March, Civil Disobedience → 1931 Gandhi–Irwin Pact → 1932 Poona Pact
1935 Government of India Act → 1942 Cripps Mission, Quit India
1943 INA under Netaji → 1946 Cabinet Mission → 15 August 1947 Independence

notes.p:
**Sample.** Consider: 1. The Lucknow Pact was signed in 1916. 2. The Poona Pact was signed between Gandhi and Jinnah. Which is/are correct? Statement 1 is correct; statement 2 is wrong — the Poona Pact (1932) was between **Gandhi and Ambedkar**. Answer: **1 only**.

Typical traps: confusing the first Governor-General of Bengal (Hastings) with the first of India (Bentinck); assuming the first Viceroy was Lord Mountbatten (it was Canning; Mountbatten was the last); and mixing up who founded Arya Samaj and Brahmo Samaj.
Turn each line into a flashcard for spaced revision.
points: Ripon = local self-government; Curzon = Partition of Bengal
Brahmo Samaj 1828; Arya Samaj 1875; Ramakrishna Mission 1897
Kesari — Tilak; Young India — Gandhi; Al-Hilal — Azad

cards.title: The President
cards.body: Elected by an electoral college of elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs of the states and of the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry. Term of 5 years. Removed by impeachment under **Article 61** for violation of the Constitution. Can grant pardons under Article 72.

cards.title: Parliament
cards.body: Lok Sabha is the House of the People; Rajya Sabha is the Council of States, a permanent body where **one-third of members retire every two years**. The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. A joint sitting (Art. 108) is presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker.

cards.title: Money bills
cards.body: Defined in **Article 110**. A money bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a money bill. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes and must return it within 14 days.

cards.title: Constitutional bodies
points: Art. 315: Union and State Public Service Commissions

cards.title: Judiciary
cards.body: The Supreme Court has original, appellate and advisory (Art. 143) jurisdiction. Writs: habeas corpus (produce the body), mandamus (we command), prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto (by what authority). High Courts can issue writs under Art. 226.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Use M. Laxmikanth-style chapter lists but start from NCERT Class 11 'Indian Constitution at Work'. Most CDS polity questions are on Parliament, the President, Fundamental Rights and constitutional bodies.

cards.q: Who decides whether a bill is a money bill?
cards.explain: Under Article 110(3), the Speaker's decision on a money bill is final.

cards.q: The Election Commission of India is provided for in:
cards.explain: Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the Election Commission.

cards.q: Which writ literally means 'to have the body'?
cards.explain: Habeas corpus orders a detained person to be produced before the court.

notes.p:
CDS polity questions test **articles, institutions, procedures and landmark amendments**, often through statement-based options. Use M. Laxmikanth's book or NCERT Political Science (Class 11 "Indian Constitution at Work") as the base, and always connect an article to the institution it creates.

Start with the structure: the Constitution has a Preamble, Parts, Articles and **12 Schedules**. Part III holds Fundamental Rights, Part IV the Directive Principles, Part IVA the Fundamental Duties, Part V the Union, Part VI the States and Parts IX and IXA the panchayats and municipalities.

The **President** can issue **ordinances** when Parliament is not in session (**Art 123**) and has the power to **pardon** (**Art 72**). The President's veto over ordinary bills can be **absolute**, **suspensive** (return the bill once) or **pocket** (keep it pending — no time limit is fixed). A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration.

**Parliament:** the **quorum** is one-tenth of the total members of a House. **Question Hour** is the first hour of a sitting; **Zero Hour**, which follows it, is an Indian parliamentary innovation not mentioned in the rules. The Rajya Sabha can delay a **Money Bill** for at most **14 days**. Under **Art 249**, Parliament can make laws on a State List subject if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

Types of bills: ordinary, money (Art 110), financial and constitutional amendment (Art 368). There is **no joint sitting** for Money Bills or constitutional amendments.

The **Governor** is appointed by the President (Art 155) and holds office during the President's pleasure. Only a few states have a **Legislative Council** (bicameral legislature); Parliament can create or abolish one on a resolution of the state assembly (Art 169).

The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave constitutional status to **Panchayati Raj** with a three-tier system (village, intermediate, district) for most states and reserved one-third of seats for women. The **74th Amendment** did the same for urban local bodies.

**Citizenship** is in Part II (Arts 5–11); details are in the **Citizenship Act, 1955**. India has **single citizenship**, borrowed from the UK.
A frequent question asks which body is constitutional. Keep three boxes:
points: Constitutional: Election Commission (Art 324), UPSC (Art 315), CAG (Art 148), Finance Commission (Art 280), Attorney General (Art 76), GST Council (Art 279A)
Statutory (created by an Act): National Human Rights Commission (1993), National Green Tribunal, Lokpal
Executive (by government resolution): NITI Aayog (2015), which replaced the Planning Commission
National Commissions for SCs (Art 338) and STs (Art 338A) are constitutional

notes.p: These come up repeatedly:
points: 44th (1978): Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights
61st: voting age 21 → 18; 86th (2002): Art 21A, right to education
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): basic structure doctrine; Maneka Gandhi (1978): wider reading of Art 21
2019: Art 370 provisions made inoperative; Jammu & Kashmir reorganised into two Union Territories

notes.p: Learn the article number together with the body it creates.
points: Quorum = one-tenth; Zero Hour is an Indian innovation
Rajya Sabha can hold a Money Bill for 14 days only
No joint sitting for Money Bills or amendments
NITI Aayog is executive; NHRC is statutory; ECI is constitutional

cards.title: World at a glance
cards.body: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean. The Nile is traditionally listed as the longest river; the Amazon carries the most water. The Sahara is the largest hot desert. Mount Everest (Nepal–China border) is the highest peak above sea level.

cards.title: Important straits
points: Hormuz: Persian Gulf ↔ Gulf of Oman (Iran–Oman)
Malacca: Andaman Sea ↔ South China Sea (Malaysia–Sumatra)

cards.title: Indian mountain passes and peaks
cards.body: Important passes: Zoji La (Srinagar–Leh), Nathu La (Sikkim–Tibet), Shipki La (Himachal–Tibet), Bomdi La (Arunachal). Kangchenjunga in Sikkim is the highest peak located within India's undisputed territory. These border regions are frequently asked in defence exams.

cards.title: Indian resources
cards.body: Jharkhand and Odisha lead in many minerals such as iron ore and coal. Major ports include Mumbai, JNPA (Navi Mumbai), Kandla/Deendayal (Gujarat), Chennai, Visakhapatnam and Kolkata/Haldia. Tea grows in Assam and West Bengal; coffee mainly in Karnataka.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Learn geography with a map, not only notes. Straits, passes and grasslands are classic match-the-following questions in CDS — a single page of tables can fetch 3–4 marks.

cards.q: The Pampas grasslands are found in:
cards.explain: The Pampas are the temperate grasslands of Argentina (and Uruguay).

cards.q: The Strait of Gibraltar connects:
cards.explain: Gibraltar links the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, between Spain and Morocco.

cards.q: Zoji La pass connects:
cards.explain: Zoji La lies on the Srinagar–Leh road in the Himalayas.

notes.p: CDS likes "largest, longest, deepest" questions and map-based matching. Core facts:
points: Largest and deepest ocean: Pacific; its Mariana Trench is the deepest point on Earth
Highest peak: Mount Everest (8,848.86 m per the 2020 China–Nepal measurement)
Longest river: the Nile (by most measurements); largest by volume of water: the Amazon
Largest hot desert: Sahara; deepest lake: Baikal (Russia); largest lake by area: Caspian Sea
Largest freshwater lake by area: Lake Superior

notes.p: Matching questions pair water bodies with the lands they separate:
points: Strait of Gibraltar: Europe (Spain) and Africa (Morocco)
Strait of Malacca: Malay Peninsula and Sumatra — a key shipping route
Strait of Hormuz: Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Bering Strait: Asia (Russia) and North America (Alaska)
Suez Canal: Mediterranean and Red Sea; Panama Canal: Atlantic and Pacific
Temperate grasslands: Prairies (N. America), Pampas (Argentina), Steppes (Eurasia), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia)

notes.p:
Revise climate types with an example region: **equatorial** (hot, wet all year — Amazon, Congo), **monsoon** (seasonal reversal of winds — South Asia), **Mediterranean** (dry summers, **rain in winter** — California, central Chile, southern Europe; famous for citrus and grapes), **hot desert** (Sahara, Thar), and **tundra** (very cold, short summer).

Other concepts: the **Coriolis effect** deflects winds right in the Northern Hemisphere; **El Niño** is the unusual warming of the eastern Pacific that often weakens the Indian monsoon; **jet streams** are fast upper-air winds. Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrate along plate boundaries such as the Pacific Ring of Fire.
High-yield Indian geography for CDS:
points: Coal: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh; Iron ore: Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka
Digboi (Assam): one of the oldest oil refineries; Mumbai High: offshore oil field
Bhakra Nangal — Sutlej; Hirakud — Mahanadi; Sardar Sarovar — Narmada; Tehri — Bhagirathi; Nagarjuna Sagar — Krishna
Corbett (Uttarakhand): India's first national park (1936); Kaziranga (Assam): one-horned rhino; Gir (Gujarat): Asiatic lion; Sundarbans: mangroves and Royal Bengal tiger

notes.p:
Spend 10 minutes daily with an atlas. When you read a news item about a place, find it on the map and note neighbouring countries and water bodies — CDS often asks "which of these countries does NOT border X?" or "arrange from north to south".

Traps: Mediterranean climates get **winter** rain, not summer rain; the Amazon carries the most water but the Nile is usually listed as longest; and the Narmada and Tapi flow **west**, unlike most peninsular rivers.
Revise with an atlas open.
points: Pacific: largest and deepest; Mariana Trench
Gibraltar, Malacca, Hormuz, Bering — know both sides
El Niño often weakens the Indian monsoon
Dams and rivers: Bhakra–Sutlej, Hirakud–Mahanadi, Tehri–Bhagirathi
Kaziranga rhino; Gir lion; Corbett first national park

cards.title: Key institutions
cards.body: The **Reserve Bank of India** was established on 1 April 1935 and nationalised in 1949; it is India's central bank and issues currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, which the Government issues). **NITI Aayog** replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

cards.title: Monetary policy terms
points: Repo rate: rate at which RBI lends to banks short-term
Reverse repo: rate at which RBI absorbs money from banks
CRR: share of deposits banks keep with RBI as cash
SLR: share of deposits banks keep in liquid assets like gold and government securities
Higher repo/CRR → less money in the economy → helps control inflation

cards.title: Inflation and the MPC
cards.body: India follows inflation targeting. The Monetary Policy Committee sets the repo rate with a target for **CPI inflation of 4%**, within a tolerance band of 2%–6%. CPI measures retail prices; WPI measures wholesale prices.

cards.title: Budget and fiscal terms
points: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings
Direct taxes: income tax, corporate tax
Indirect tax: GST — launched 1 July 2017 (101st Amendment)

cards.title: Planning and sectors
cards.body: The First Five Year Plan ran from 1951 to 1956 and focused on agriculture. The economy has primary (agriculture, mining), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services) sectors; services contribute the largest share of India's GDP.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: CDS economy questions are conceptual. NCERT Class 9–12 Economics plus the Economic Survey highlights (free on the Finance Ministry website) are enough. Understand what each term does — don't just memorise definitions.

cards.q: The repo rate is the rate at which:
cards.explain: Repo is RBI's short-term lending rate to banks against government securities.

cards.q: GST was introduced in India on:
cards.explain: GST came into effect on 1 July 2017 after the 101st Constitutional Amendment.

cards.q: NITI Aayog replaced which body?
cards.explain: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

notes.p:
**GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** is the value of all final goods and services produced **within** a country's borders in a year. **GNP** = GDP + net factor income from abroad. **NNP** = GNP − depreciation. National income in the strict sense is NNP at **factor cost**. **Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** uses constant (base-year) prices, so it removes the effect of inflation.

The economy has three sectors: **primary** (agriculture, mining), **secondary** (manufacturing, construction) and **tertiary** (services). In India, the services sector contributes the largest share of GDP, while agriculture still employs a very large share of workers.

**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level. **Demand-pull** inflation comes from too much demand; **cost-push** from rising input costs (like fuel). **Deflation** is falling prices; **stagflation** is high inflation with low growth. India's headline inflation measure for policy is the **CPI** (retail); the **WPI** measures wholesale prices.

The **Monetary Policy Committee** (six members — three from the RBI including the Governor, and three external) sets the repo rate. The inflation target has been **4% CPI with a band of 2%–6%** (check for any revision of the framework).
points: Repo rate: RBI lends to banks short-term against securities
CRR: share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI as cash
SLR: share of deposits banks keep in liquid assets (gold, government securities)
To fight inflation the RBI usually raises rates (tight money); to boost growth it cuts them

notes.h: Budget and fiscal terms with an example
notes.p: The Budget is the **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112**. Key deficits:
points: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments
Example: total expenditure ₹100, receipts excluding borrowings ₹80 → fiscal deficit ₹20. If interest payments are ₹8, primary deficit = 20 − 8 = ₹12
Direct taxes: income tax, corporation tax; indirect: GST (from 1 July 2017, 101st Amendment)

notes.p:
Major milestones: the **RBI** was set up on 1 April 1935 and nationalised in 1949; **14 major banks were nationalised in 1969** and six more in 1980; **NABARD** was set up in 1982 for rural credit; **SEBI** regulates the securities market (statutory since 1992). The **1991 reforms** — liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG) — were introduced when P.V. Narasimha Rao was Prime Minister and Manmohan Singh Finance Minister.

**Planning:** the First Five Year Plan (1951–56) focused on agriculture; the Second (Mahalanobis model) on heavy industry. **NITI Aayog** replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

**International:** the **IMF and World Bank** arose from the Bretton Woods Conference (1944); the **WTO** (1995) replaced GATT and is headquartered in Geneva. The **Human Development Index** is published by the UNDP.

Don't confuse **fiscal policy** (government taxing and spending) with **monetary policy** (RBI controlling money and interest rates). Remember that a higher CRR **reduces** the money banks can lend. Growth numbers, rankings and budget figures change every year — for these, check the latest Economic Survey and Budget documents rather than memorising old values.

Study with NCERT Economics (Class 9–12), then read the Economic Survey's summary chapter each year.
Concepts matter more than numbers in CDS economy.
points: GDP within borders; GNP adds net factor income from abroad
Real GDP removes inflation; nominal does not
CPI target 4% (2–6%) set by a six-member MPC
Higher repo/CRR → less money → lower inflation
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 Jan 2015

cards.title: Physics in daily life
cards.body: The Sun produces energy by **nuclear fusion** (hydrogen into helium); nuclear power plants use **fission** of uranium. The electromagnetic spectrum, from long to short wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

cards.title: Chemistry facts
cards.body: Noble gases (helium, neon, argon…) are chemically inert. Helium is used in balloons because it is light and non-flammable. LPG is mainly butane and propane; CNG is mainly methane. Ozone (O₃) protects us from UV radiation.

cards.title: Biology facts
cards.body: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using sunlight and chlorophyll. DNA carries genetic information. **Rhizobium** bacteria in the root nodules of legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen, which improves soil fertility.

cards.title: Space and India
cards.body: ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 made India the first country to soft-land near the Moon's south polar region, on 23 August 2023 (now National Space Day). Aditya-L1, launched in September 2023, is India's first space-based solar observatory, placed around the Sun–Earth L1 point.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Science questions in CDS are mostly 'why' and 'what is used for' questions. NCERT Class 6–10 Science covers most of them. Add ISRO and DRDO news from PIB for the technology part.

cards.q: Brass is an alloy of:
cards.explain: Brass is copper with zinc; bronze is copper with tin.

cards.q: The Sun's energy is produced by:
cards.explain: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing energy.

cards.q: Which bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes?
cards.explain: Rhizobium lives in legume root nodules and converts atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms.

notes.p: CDS science asks "why" questions from daily life. Know the principle behind each:
points: Lightning is seen before thunder is heard — light travels far faster than sound
A pressure cooker cooks faster — higher pressure raises the boiling point of water
Salt is spread on icy roads — dissolved salt lowers the freezing point
Ice floats — it is less dense than liquid water
The sky is blue — air scatters shorter (blue) wavelengths more
A straw seems bent in water — refraction
Nuclear reactors use fission; the Sun's energy comes from fusion of hydrogen into helium

notes.p: Common compounds: baking soda (NaHCO₃) makes cakes rise by releasing CO₂; washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) softens water; bleaching powder (CaOCl₂) disinfects water; plaster of Paris sets into gypsum when mixed with water. Soaps clean by forming micelles around grease. **Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts; it doesn't lather well with soap. **Rusting** needs oxygen and moisture and is prevented by painting, oiling or galvanising (zinc coating). LPG is mostly butane/propane; CNG mostly methane. **Ozone** in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV radiation; CFCs damage it.

Key ideas: the cell is the unit of life; DNA carries genetic information; humans have 46 chromosomes. **Vitamins:** A (night blindness), B1 (beriberi), C (scurvy), D (rickets), K (clotting). **Diseases by cause:** bacterial — TB, cholera, typhoid; viral — polio, measles, rabies, AIDS, dengue, COVID-19; protozoan — malaria. **Antibiotics** work against bacteria, not viruses. Insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar. Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts and releases oxygen.
**ISRO** was set up in 1969. Milestones worth knowing:
points: Aryabhata (1975): India's first satellite, launched by the Soviet Union
Chandrayaan-1 (2008): its instruments helped confirm water molecules on the Moon
Mangalyaan / Mars Orbiter Mission: launched 2013, reached Mars orbit in 2014 on its first attempt
Chandrayaan-3: Vikram lander touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023 (now National Space Day); the Pragyan rover explored the surface
Aditya-L1 (launched 2023): India's first solar observatory mission, placed near the Sun–Earth L1 point
Launch vehicles: PSLV (workhorse for polar orbits), GSLV and LVM3 (heavier payloads)
Computing basics: 1 byte = 8 bits; RAM is volatile, ROM is not; CPU = brain of the computer

notes.p:
Instruments: **barometer** (atmospheric pressure), **hygrometer** (humidity), **anemometer** (wind speed), **seismograph** (earthquakes), **lactometer** (purity of milk), **ammeter** (current), **voltmeter** (voltage), **odometer** (distance travelled by a vehicle).

Discoveries: **penicillin** — Alexander Fleming; **telephone** — Alexander Graham Bell; **theory of relativity** — Albert Einstein; **Raman effect** — C.V. Raman (Nobel Prize 1930; National Science Day is 28 February); **radioactivity** — Henri Becquerel; **electron** — J.J. Thomson.

Trap: "anemometer" (wind speed) and "ammeter" (current) sound alike — read options carefully.
One-line reasons win easy marks in CDS science.
points: Pressure cooker: higher pressure, higher boiling point
Salt on ice lowers the freezing point
Chandrayaan-3 landing: 23 August 2023, near the lunar south pole
Raman effect: Nobel 1930; Science Day 28 Feb

cards.title: The three services
cards.body: Army motto: 'Service Before Self'. Navy motto: 'Sham No Varunah' (May the Lord of the Waters be auspicious unto us). Air Force motto: 'Nabhah Sprisham Deeptam' (Touch the sky with glory), from the Bhagavad Gita. The post of **Chief of Defence Staff** was created in 2019; Gen Bipin Rawat was the first CDS.

cards.title: Important days
points: Air Force Day: 8 October (IAF formed in 1932)

cards.title: Gallantry awards
cards.body: Wartime (in order): **Param Vir Chakra**, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra. Peacetime: **Ashoka Chakra**, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra. The first Param Vir Chakra was awarded to Major Somnath Sharma (1947, posthumous).

notes.p:
The **President of India** is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces. The **Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)**, a post created in 2019, heads the **Department of Military Affairs** in the Ministry of Defence; **Gen Bipin Rawat** was the first CDS (from 1 January 2020). For current service chiefs and the current CDS, check the latest Ministry of Defence releases, as these change.

Army ranks in order: Lieutenant, Captain, Major, Lieutenant Colonel, Colonel, Brigadier, Major General, Lieutenant General, General. Navy: Sub Lieutenant, Lieutenant, Lieutenant Commander, Commander, Captain, Commodore, Rear Admiral, Vice Admiral, Admiral. Five-star ranks: **Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw** (first, 1973) and **Field Marshal K.M. Cariappa** (1986); **Marshal of the IAF Arjan Singh**.

**Gallantry awards:** wartime — Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra; peacetime — Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra. The first PVC was awarded posthumously to **Major Somnath Sharma** (1947). **Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon** is the only IAF recipient of the PVC.

Abdul Kalam, produced Prithvi, Agni, Akash, Trishul and Nag. **BrahMos** (named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers) is an India–Russia supersonic cruise missile; **Astra** is an air-to-air missile.

**Platforms:** **INS Vikrant** — India's first indigenous aircraft carrier (commissioned 2022); **INS Vikramaditya** — ex-Russian carrier; **INS Arihant** — first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine; **Tejas** — light combat aircraft; **Arjun** — main battle tank; **Pinaka** — multi-barrel rocket launcher.

cards.body: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere, between about **8°4′N and 37°6′N** (mainland) and **68°7′E and 97°25′E**. The **Tropic of Cancer** (23.5°N) passes through eight states. Indian Standard Time is based on **82.5°E**.

notes.p:
The CDS GK syllabus says geography questions will be of a level an educated person can answer "without special study" — so the basics of India's physical geography come up often.

India is the **seventh largest** country by area. Its mainland stretches about 3,214 km north–south and 2,933 km east–west. The Tropic of Cancer passes through **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram**. The southernmost point of India is **Indira Point** in the Great Nicobar island; the southernmost point of the mainland is Kanyakumari.
points: Neighbours with longest land border: Bangladesh
Palk Strait separates India and Sri Lanka
Ten Degree Channel separates Andaman and Nicobar

notes.p:
The Himalaya has three parallel ranges: the **Greater Himalaya (Himadri)**, the **Lesser Himalaya (Himachal)** and the **Shiwaliks**. Longitudinal valleys between Himachal and Shiwalik are called **duns** (Dehradun). **Kangchenjunga** (Sikkim–Nepal border) is the highest peak in the Indian-administered Himalaya; NCERT lists **K2 (Godwin Austen)**, in territory claimed by India, as India's highest peak — read options carefully.

The northern plains are built by alluvium from the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems. **Bhabar** is the pebble belt at the foothills; **Terai** is the marshy belt south of it; **Bhangar** is older alluvium and **Khadar** newer, more fertile alluvium.

notes.h: Peninsular plateau, desert, coasts and islands
notes.p:
The peninsular plateau is one of the oldest landmasses, divided into the **Central Highlands** and the **Deccan Plateau**. The **Western Ghats** are higher and continuous; the **Eastern Ghats** are lower and broken by rivers. **Anamudi** is the highest peak of south India.

The western coastal plain is narrow (Konkan, Kannad, Malabar); the eastern coastal plain is wider (Northern Circars, Coromandel). **Lakshadweep** islands are coral in origin; the **Andaman and Nicobar** islands are an extension of submerged mountains, and **Barren Island** has India's only active volcano.

Himalayan rivers are snow- and rain-fed, so they flow all year. Peninsular rivers are rain-fed and seasonal in flow.

• The Ganga is formed at **Devprayag** by the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda.
• The Brahmaputra is called Tsangpo in Tibet and enters India in Arunachal Pradesh.
• The Narmada rises at **Amarkantak** and flows west between the Vindhya and Satpura.
• Wular (J&K) is among India's largest freshwater lakes; Chilika (Odisha) is a large brackish-water lagoon.

India has a **tropical monsoon** climate. The monsoon arrives on the Kerala coast around the start of June and normally covers the country by early-to-mid July (check IMD for current dates). **Mawsynram** and **Cherrapunji** in Meghalaya receive some of the highest rainfall in the world; western Rajasthan receives the least.

Soils follow geology and rainfall: **alluvial** in the plains, **black** in the lava-covered Deccan, **red and yellow** on old crystalline rocks, **laterite** where heavy rain leaches nutrients, and **desert** soils in Rajasthan.

points: Force: newton; work/energy: joule; power: watt
Current: ampere; resistance: ohm; charge: coulomb

cards.title: Newton's laws
cards.body: 1st: a body stays at rest or uniform motion unless a net force acts (**inertia**). 2nd: F = ma. 3rd: every action has an equal and opposite reaction — the principle of **rockets and jet engines**.

cards.title: Light
cards.body: Light travels at about **3 × 10⁸ m/s** in vacuum. **Refraction** makes a pool look shallower and causes twinkling of stars. **Dispersion** splits white light (rainbow). The sky is blue because of **scattering** of shorter wavelengths. Total internal reflection works in **optical fibres** and causes mirages.

cards.title: Sound
cards.body: Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through vacuum. It is fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. Humans hear about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**; above that is **ultrasound** (used in SONAR and medical scans).

cards.title: Electricity
points: Household supply in India: 220–230 V, 50 Hz AC

cards.title: Defence link
cards.body: Many questions link physics to defence technology: **radar** uses radio waves, **SONAR** uses sound underwater, **night vision** uses infrared, and jet propulsion uses Newton's third law.

cards.q: The SI unit of power is:
The sky appears blue because of:
cards.explain: Shorter blue wavelengths are scattered more by air molecules.

cards.q: Sound cannot travel through:
cards.explain: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium.

notes.p:
The CDS GK syllabus asks for the scientific side of "matters of everyday observation and experience". In physics that means simple mechanics, heat, light, sound, electricity and magnetism.

**Inertia** explains why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes. **Momentum** p = mv; a gun recoils because total momentum is conserved. **Friction** lets us walk; ball bearings reduce it. Weight is mg and changes with g; **mass does not change** from place to place. Weight is zero in free fall (astronauts in orbit feel weightless).
points: g is slightly more at the poles than at the equator

notes.p:
Work = force × displacement in the direction of force. Energy changes form but is conserved: a falling body converts potential energy to kinetic energy.

**Pressure** = force/area: a sharp knife cuts better (small area), and camels' broad feet help them walk on sand. **Pascal's law** underlies hydraulic brakes and lifts. **Archimedes' principle** explains floating ships; a body floats if its density is less than the liquid's. **Bernoulli's principle** explains aircraft lift: faster air over the curved upper surface means lower pressure.

Heat flows from hot to cold by **conduction**, **convection** and **radiation**. Sea and land breezes are convection currents. Water expands on freezing, which is why pipes burst in winter and ice floats. Water has the maximum density at **4°C**.

Temperature conversions: °F = (9/5)°C + 32; K = °C + 273. **−40** is the same in Celsius and Fahrenheit. Normal body temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F).

Mirrors and lenses: a **concave mirror** is used in shaving mirrors and headlights; a **convex mirror** gives a wide view, so it is used as a rear-view mirror. **Myopia** (short sight) is corrected with a concave lens; **hypermetropia** with a convex lens.

Sound echo needs a minimum distance of about **17 m** at normal speed. The **Doppler effect** changes the observed frequency of a moving source and is used in police radar guns and weather radar. Bats navigate by ultrasound echoes.

Fuses melt when current is too high; they have low melting point and are connected in **series**. Household appliances are connected in **parallel** so each gets full voltage. An **electric motor** converts electrical energy to mechanical; a **generator (dynamo)** does the reverse by **electromagnetic induction** (Faraday). A **transformer** works only with AC.

**Worked example.** A 1,000 W heater runs 3 hours a day for 30 days. Energy = 1 kW × 90 h = **90 kWh (units)**.
Physics one-liners.

Blue sky: scattering; mirage: total internal reflection

cards.title: Matter and acids
cards.body: Acids turn blue litmus red and have pH < 7; bases turn red litmus blue and have pH > 7. Pure water has pH 7. Vinegar contains **acetic acid**; lemon has **citric acid**; stomach makes **hydrochloric acid**; ant sting has **formic acid**.

cards.title: Metals and alloys
cards.body: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature. **Brass** = copper + zinc; **bronze** = copper + tin; **stainless steel** = iron + chromium (+ nickel); **solder** = lead + tin. Rusting of iron needs both oxygen and water.

cards.title: Human body
cards.body: Largest organ: **skin**; largest gland: **liver**; smallest bone: **stapes** (ear). Adult humans have **206 bones**. Red blood cells carry oxygen using **haemoglobin**; platelets help clotting; white cells fight infection.

cards.title: Diseases by cause
cards.body: Virus: polio, measles, rabies, COVID-19, AIDS. Bacteria: tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus. Protozoa: malaria (Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquito). Many quiz questions just ask the cause.

cards.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
Brass is an alloy of:
Malaria is caused by a:

notes.p:
Questions test familiar substances and reactions. **Acids** release H⁺ in water; **bases** release OH⁻; their reaction gives salt and water (**neutralisation**) — the reason antacids (bases like magnesium hydroxide) relieve acidity, and baking soda soothes an ant bite.

**pH** runs from 0 to 14. Blood is slightly basic (about 7.4). Acid rain is caused mainly by oxides of **sulphur** and **nitrogen**.
points: Rusting is oxidation; galvanising coats iron with zinc
LPG is mainly butane and propane; CNG is mainly methane

notes.p:
The most abundant element in the Earth's crust is **oxygen**; the most abundant metal there is **aluminium**. The atmosphere is about **78% nitrogen** and **21% oxygen**. Diamond and graphite are both forms of **carbon**: diamond is the hardest natural substance, graphite conducts electricity and is a lubricant.

Noble gases are unreactive: helium is used in balloons, neon in advertising lights, argon in bulbs. **Sodium** is stored in kerosene because it reacts violently with air and water.

Common names often asked: **laughing gas** is nitrous oxide (N₂O); **marsh gas** is methane; **heavy water** is D₂O, used as a moderator in some nuclear reactors; **quicklime** is calcium oxide and **slaked lime** is calcium hydroxide.

The **cell** is the basic unit of life; the **mitochondrion** is the "powerhouse"; the **nucleus** holds DNA. Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

The **heart** has four chambers; arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, an exception). **Insulin**, made by the pancreas, controls blood sugar; its deficiency causes diabetes. The **kidneys** filter blood; the **nephron** is their unit. Blood groups: O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient (for red cells).

Carbohydrates and fats give energy; proteins build tissue; vitamins and minerals regulate body functions. **Fat-soluble** vitamins are A, D, E and K; B and C are water-soluble. Vitamin D is made by the skin in sunlight.

**Vaccines** train immunity; antibiotics work against bacteria, **not viruses**. **Penicillin** was discovered by Alexander Fleming. India was declared polio-free by the WHO (South-East Asia region certification in 2014).

Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. **Nitrogen fixation** by bacteria in legume root nodules enriches soil. Food chains run from producers to consumers; energy reduces at each level (roughly 10% passes on).

**Worked recall chain:** pulses → root nodules → Rhizobium → nitrogen fixation → less need for urea. Questions often take one link of this chain.
Chem-bio one-liners.
points: Baking soda NaHCO₃; washing soda Na₂CO₃
Crust: O most; Al most abundant metal

cards.title: What CDS expects
cards.body: The official syllabus includes "knowledge of **current events**". Questions cover national and international events, defence news, appointments, summits, awards, sports and science and technology from roughly the past year.

cards.title: Sources that work
points: One national newspaper daily (editorial + national pages)
PIB (pib.gov.in) for government schemes and defence releases
A monthly current-affairs compilation for revision

cards.title: Static-current link
cards.body: Current events become questions through static facts: a summit question asks the host city; a mission launch asks the launch vehicle; a new appointment asks about the office in the Constitution. Always revise the **static background** of each news item.

cards.title: Categories to track
points: Defence: exercises, inductions, appointments of chiefs
Economy: budget, RBI policy terms, schemes

cards.title: Note format
cards.body: One line per item: **What – Who – Where – Why it matters – Static link**. E.g. an exercise: name, partner country, location, service, and earlier editions if any.

cards.title: Verify, don't memorise rumours
cards.body: Use only official or reputable sources; numbers and rankings change every year. For anything you are unsure of, check the latest notification or official release rather than relying on social-media summaries.

cards.q: Which official source publishes Government of India press releases?
cards.explain: The Press Information Bureau issues official press releases.

cards.q: The best way to remember a news item for GK is to:
options: link it to static facts (place, body, constitution)
cards.explain: Questions usually test the static fact behind the news.

cards.q: Which of these is a UN body headquartered in Geneva?
cards.explain: WHO is headquartered in Geneva; UNICEF in New York, UNESCO in Paris, FAO in Rome.

notes.p:
The CDS General Knowledge paper explicitly includes **current events**, and a sizeable share of questions in recent papers relate to recent developments — exact numbers vary by paper. Unlike static GK, this portion changes every cycle, so it rewards regular habits rather than last-minute cramming.

Cover roughly the 12 months before the exam date.
points: Read daily, revise weekly, consolidate monthly
Note official names and abbreviations correctly

notes.p:
**Step 1 (20 minutes):** Read national news and one editorial; underline events likely to be asked (schemes, appointments, exercises, launches).
**Step 2 (10 minutes):** Write one-line notes in the What–Who–Where–Why format.
**Step 3 (weekly):** Revise the week's notes and add static links (headquarters, constitutional articles, earlier editions).
**Step 4 (monthly):** Solve 50–100 current-affairs MCQs from a monthly compilation.

This takes about 30 minutes a day and builds a compact revision file.

Many current questions anchor to organisations. Know headquarters and purpose:
• **UN** — New York; **WHO**, **WTO**, **ILO** — Geneva
• **UNESCO** — Paris; **FAO** — Rome; **IAEA** — Vienna
• **IMF** and **World Bank** — Washington, D.C.
• **ASEAN** secretariat — Jakarta; **SAARC** secretariat — Kathmandu
• **NATO** — Brussels; **International Court of Justice** — The Hague

When a summit is in the news, add the host, the theme and India's role to your notes.

Also keep a short list of India-related groupings: **BRICS**, **SCO**, **G20**, **Quad**, **BIMSTEC** and **IBSA** — member countries, and where the most recent summit was held (check the latest edition before the exam).

Defence news is particularly useful for CDS. Track: bilateral and multilateral **exercises** (name, partner, service), **inductions** of new platforms, **indigenous** projects, and **appointments** (Chief of Defence Staff, service chiefs). Use the Ministry of Defence and PIB defence releases as the primary source. Because names of exercises and appointments change, always confirm the latest status before the exam.

Do not rely on memory for numbers like rankings and indices — they change each year, and options are often previous years' values. If two options look right, the question is usually testing the most recent edition. Skip a current-affairs question you genuinely do not know; with negative marking, guessing between four unfamiliar names rarely pays.

**Worked example of linking.** Suppose the news says ISRO launched a satellite. Possible questions: the launch vehicle family (PSLV, GSLV, LVM3), the launch centre (Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota), the orbit type (polar sun-synchronous vs geostationary) and the purpose of the mission. One news item can generate four static questions, which is why notes must include the background.
Current affairs plan.
points: Cover about 12 months before the exam
Know HQs: WHO Geneva, UNESCO Paris, IMF Washington
Confirm latest facts from official sources

points: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
Divisible by 3 or 9: sum of digits divisible by 3 or 9
Divisible by 11: (sum of odd-place digits − sum of even-place digits) is 0 or a multiple of 11

cards.title: Percentage, profit & loss

Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% = 28% overall

cards.title: Time, speed, work

If A takes a days and B takes b days, together: ab/(a + b) days

cards.title: Work together
cards.body: A finishes a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. Together they do 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the job per day, so they finish in **6 days** (check: 10×15/25 = 6).

cards.title: Compound interest
cards.body: ₹10,000 at 10% per annum, compounded yearly, for 2 years: Amount = 10,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹12,100. CI = **₹2,100**. SI would be ₹2,000, and the ₹100 difference = 10,000 × (0.1)².

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: CDS Maths is 100 questions in 2 hours — just over a minute each. Arithmetic is the most scoring part. Learn tables to 25, squares to 30 and cubes to 15 to speed up calculations.

cards.q: Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
The HCF of two numbers is 12 and the LCM is 72. If one number is 24, the other is:
An article bought for ₹400 is sold for ₹500. The profit percentage is:

notes.p:
**Natural numbers** start at 1; **whole numbers** include 0; **integers** include negatives; **rational numbers** can be written p/q (q ≠ 0); **irrational numbers** (√2, π) cannot. Every terminating or recurring decimal is rational. A **prime** has exactly two factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime.

**Number of factors:** write N = aᵖ × bᵠ × …, then factors = (p + 1)(q + 1)…. For 72 = 2³ × 3², factors = 4 × 3 = **12**.

**Recurring decimals:** 0.3̄ = 3/9 = 1/3; 0.2̄7̄ (27 repeating) = 27/99 = **3/11**.
points: Divisible by 3 or 9: sum of digits divisible by 3 or 9
By 4: last two digits; by 8: last three digits
By 11: difference between sums of alternate digits is 0 or a multiple of 11
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers

notes.h: HCF, LCM, unit digits and remainders
notes.p:
**Example 1.** HCF and LCM of 36 and 48.
Step 1: 36 = 2² × 3², 48 = 2⁴ × 3.
Step 2: HCF = lowest powers = 2² × 3 = **12**. LCM = highest powers = 2⁴ × 3² = **144**.
Check: 12 × 144 = 1728 = 36 × 48. ✓

**Example 2.** Unit digit of 7⁹⁵.
Step 1: Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1 — a cycle of 4.
Step 2: 95 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 3.
Step 3: Third in the cycle = **3**.

LCM is used for "when will bells ring together" problems; HCF for "largest size of tile/container" problems.

Percentage change = (change/original) × 100. Profit and loss % are always on **cost price** unless stated otherwise.

**Example 3.** The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family cut consumption to keep spending the same?
Step 1: Reduction % = rise/(100 + rise) × 100.
Step 2: = 25/125 × 100 = **20%**.

**Example 4.** An article bought for ₹400 is sold for ₹500. Profit = 100, profit % = 100/400 × 100 = **25%**.

SI = PRT/100. CI: Amount = P(1 + R/100)ᵀ, and CI = Amount − P.

**Example 5.** P = ₹10,000, R = 10% per annum, T = 2 years.
Step 1: SI = 10,000 × 10 × 2/100 = ₹2,000.
Step 2: Amount = 10,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹12,100, so CI = ₹2,100.
Step 3: Difference = ₹100. Shortcut for 2 years: P(R/100)² = 10,000 × 0.01 = **₹100**. ✓

**Example 6.** A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. Together?
Step 1: Per-day work = 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36.
Step 2: Days = 36/5 = **7.2 days**.

**Example 7.** A 150 m train runs at 54 km/h. How long to pass a pole?
Step 1: 54 km/h × 5/18 = 15 m/s.
Step 2: Time = 150/15 = **10 s**.

Traps: forgetting to convert units (km/h to m/s), calculating profit % on selling price, and treating successive percentage changes as simply additive (+10% then −10% is a net **−1%**, not 0).
Write these on your rough sheet before starting the maths paper.

cards.title: Algebraic identities
points: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

cards.title: Remainder and factor theorems
cards.body: When p(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is **p(a)**. If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor. This turns long division into a 10-second substitution.

cards.title: Quadratic and linear equations
points: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ have a unique solution if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂
No solution if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂

cards.title: x + 1/x tricks
cards.body: If x + 1/x = 3, then squaring: x² + 2 + 1/x² = 9, so x² + 1/x² = **7**. Cubing: x³ + 1/x³ = (x + 1/x)³ − 3(x + 1/x) = 27 − 9 = **18**.

cards.title: Remainder theorem
cards.body: Find the remainder when x³ − 2x + 5 is divided by (x − 1). Put x = 1: 1 − 2 + 5 = **4**. No long division needed.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: In algebra, substituting simple values (x = 0, 1, 2) into both the question and options often finds the answer faster than solving. Use it whenever options contain variables.
