chapters.title: Maths: number system, square roots & decimal fractions

cards.title: Classes of numbers
cards.body: **Natural numbers** 1, 2, 3…; **whole numbers** add 0; **integers** add negatives; **rationals** are p/q with q ≠ 0; **irrationals** like √2, π cannot be written so. Rationals and irrationals together make the **real numbers**.
points: Terminating or recurring decimals are rational

cards.title: Recurring decimals to fractions
points: Non-repeating digits give 0s in the denominator; repeating digits give 9s

cards.title: Fundamental operations and BODMAS
cards.body: Simplify in the order **B**rackets, **O**f, **D**ivision, **M**ultiplication, **A**ddition, **S**ubtraction. Division and multiplication are done left to right, as are addition and subtraction. Remove brackets innermost first: ( ), then { }, then [ ].

cards.title: Square roots and surds
points: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8

cards.title: Comparing fractions fast
cards.body: To compare a/b and c/d, cross-multiply: compare ad with bc. To compare surds like √3 + √7 and √4 + √6, square both: 10 + 2√21 vs 10 + 2√24, so the second is bigger.

cards.q: Which of these is irrational?
cards.explain: √12 = 2√3, which is irrational. √49 = 7, and the others are p/q forms.

cards.q: 0.2̄7̄ (27 recurring) as a fraction is:

cards.explain: Multiply by (√3 − √2): denominator 3 − 2 = 1, so the value is √3 − √2.

notes.p:
CDS starts Elementary Mathematics from the **real number system**. Every point on the number line is a real number, and real numbers split into **rational** (p/q, q ≠ 0) and **irrational** numbers.

Natural numbers ⊂ whole numbers ⊂ integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals. Between any two rationals there are infinitely many rationals and infinitely many irrationals. The sum of a rational and an irrational is always **irrational**; the product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational. But the sum or product of two irrationals can be rational: √2 × √2 = 2.
points: 0 is a whole number but not a natural number
π and e are irrational; 22/7 is only an approximation of π

notes.p:
A fraction p/q (in lowest terms) gives a **terminating decimal** only when q has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³ × 5) but 1/12 recurs (12 has the factor 3).

**Example 1.** Convert 0.13̄ (only 3 repeating) to a fraction.
Step 1: Write all digits as a number: 13; subtract the non-repeating part: 13 − 1 = 12.
Step 2: One repeating digit → one 9; one non-repeating digit → one 0. Denominator 90.
Step 3: 12/90 = **2/15**.

When adding decimals, line up the decimal points; when multiplying, the answer has as many decimal places as the two factors together (0.3 × 0.02 = 0.006).

**Example 2.** Simplify 18 ÷ 3 × 2 + 4 of (6 − 2).
Step 1: Brackets: 6 − 2 = 4.
Step 2: Of: 4 of 4 = 16.
Step 3: Division and multiplication, left to right: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12.
Step 4: 12 + 16 = **28**.

A common trap is doing 3 × 2 first and dividing 18 by 6; that gives 3 + 16 = 19, which is wrong.

Find square roots of perfect squares by **prime factorisation** (pair the factors) or, for big numbers, by the long-division method. Unit digit rules help eliminate options: a square ending in 6 has a root ending in 4 or 6; ending in 9 → root ends in 3 or 7.

**Example 3.** Simplify 1/(√5 − 2).
Step 1: Multiply top and bottom by (√5 + 2).
Step 2: Denominator = 5 − 4 = 1.
Step 3: Value = **√5 + 2** ≈ 4.236.

For √(a + 2√b), look for two numbers x, y with x + y = a and xy = b; then it equals √x + √y. Example: √(7 + 2√10) = √5 + √2.

Students lose marks by assuming every non-terminating decimal is irrational (recurring ones are rational), by forgetting to reduce p/q to lowest terms before testing for 2s and 5s, and by mis-ordering BODMAS. In surd comparisons, always square (or rationalise) instead of estimating loosely.
Revise these before any number-system question.
points: √(a + 2√b) = √x + √y where x + y = a, xy = b

cards.title: Division algorithm
cards.body: For integers a and b > 0 there are unique integers q and r with **a = bq + r**, 0 ≤ r < b. Every remainder question uses this: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder.

cards.title: Divisibility tests
points: 2: last digit even; 5: last digit 0 or 5
11: (sum of odd-place digits − sum of even-place digits) = 0 or multiple of 11

cards.title: Primes and factorisation theorem
cards.body: A **prime** has exactly two factors; a **composite** has more. The **fundamental theorem of arithmetic (factorisation theorem)**: every integer > 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, ignoring order.
points: To test n for primality, try primes up to √n

cards.title: Factors of N = aᵖbᵠcʳ
points: HCF = lowest powers of common primes
LCM = highest powers of all primes

cards.title: HCF/LCM rules
points: Least number leaving remainder r with divisors a, b, c = LCM + r

cards.title: Which to use
cards.body: "Largest tile / biggest container / greatest number dividing exactly" → **HCF**. "Bells ring together / least number divisible / runners meet again" → **LCM**.

cards.q: Which number is divisible by 11?
cards.explain: 3421: odd places (from right) 1 + 4 = 5, even places 2 + 3 = 5; difference 0, so divisible by 11.

cards.q: Number of factors of 360 is:
Least number which when divided by 6, 8 and 12 leaves remainder 2 in each case:

notes.p:
Every remainder problem is an application of **a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b**. If a number leaves remainder 7 when divided by 12, it has the form 12k + 7; when that number is divided by 4 (a factor of 12), the remainder is the remainder of 7 ÷ 4 = **3**.

Remainders multiply and add: the remainder of (a × b) ÷ n equals the remainder of (rₐ × r_b) ÷ n. So 37 × 43 ÷ 6 → remainders 1 × 1 = **1**.
points: Remainder is always less than divisor
If the divisor is a factor of the first divisor, reduce the old remainder
Use small-remainder products to avoid big multiplication

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus names tests for **2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 11**. Combine co-prime tests for others: divisible by 6 means by 2 and 3; by 15 means by 3 and 5; by 18 means by 2 and 9.

To check if 221 is prime, try primes up to √221 ≈ 14.9: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. 221 = 13 × 17, so it is **composite**. Two numbers are **co-prime** if their HCF is 1 (8 and 15), even if neither is prime.

Because prime factorisation is unique, many questions reduce to exponents.

**Example 1.** How many factors does 720 have, and how many are even?
Step 1: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5.
Step 2: Total factors = 5 × 3 × 2 = **30**.
Step 3: Odd factors use 2⁰ only: 3 × 2 = 6.
Step 4: Even factors = 30 − 6 = **24**.

notes.h: HCF and LCM, including the Euclidean algorithm
notes.p:
HCF uses lowest common powers; LCM uses highest powers. For large numbers, the **Euclidean algorithm** is faster: divide the larger by the smaller, then the divisor by the remainder, until the remainder is 0.

**Example 2.** Find the greatest number that divides 43, 91 and 183 leaving the same remainder.
Step 1: Same remainder means the differences are exact multiples: 91 − 43 = 48, 183 − 91 = 92, 183 − 43 = 140.
Step 2: HCF(48, 92, 140): 48 = 2⁴·3, 92 = 2²·23, 140 = 2²·5·7 → HCF = 4.
Step 3: Answer **4** (each leaves remainder 3).

**Example 3.** Bells toll every 6, 8 and 15 minutes. If they toll together at 9:00, when next? LCM = 120 min → **11:00**.

HCF × LCM = product works for **two** numbers only. The HCF of fractions is HCF of numerators over **LCM** of denominators — students often swap these. For "same remainder" questions use differences, and for "different remainders r₁, r₂, r₃" subtract each remainder from its number before taking the HCF.
Key results for number theory questions.
points: HCF: lowest powers; LCM: highest powers
Euclid: repeat divide, last non-zero remainder is HCF
Remainder r with all divisors → LCM + r

cards.title: What a log is
cards.body: **log_a x = y** means aʸ = x (a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0). CDS uses **common logarithms**, base 10: log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3, log 1 = 0.

cards.title: Laws of logarithms
points: Change of base: log_a b = log b / log a

cards.title: Characteristic and mantissa
cards.body: A common log has an integer part, the **characteristic**, and a decimal part, the **mantissa** (from tables, always positive). For a number with n digits before the decimal point, characteristic = n − 1. For 0.00xyz with k zeros after the point, characteristic = −(k + 1), written k+1 with a bar.

cards.title: Digit count trick
cards.body: Number of digits in N = (characteristic of log N) + 1. 2⁵⁰: log = 50 × 0.3010 = 15.05 → characteristic 15 → **16 digits**.

cards.q: If log 2 = 0.3010, log 8 is:
log₂ 32 equals:
The characteristic of log 0.00346 is:
cards.explain: Two zeros right after the decimal point → characteristic −(2+1) = −3, written 3̄.

notes.p:
A logarithm answers "what power?". **log_a x = y ⇔ aʸ = x**. The base must be positive and not 1, and only positive numbers have real logarithms. In CDS, "log" without a base means **base 10**, the common logarithm, which the syllabus links to **use of logarithmic tables**.

Two instant facts: log of the base is 1, and log of 1 is 0 in any base.
points: Log of a negative number or zero is undefined

notes.h: The laws and why they work
notes.p:
Since logs are exponents, the exponent laws become log laws: multiplying numbers adds logs, dividing subtracts them, and powers come down as multipliers.

**Example 1.** Given log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771, find log 1.2.
Step 1: 1.2 = 12/10 = 2² × 3 / 10.
Step 2: log 1.2 = 2(0.3010) + 0.4771 − 1.
Step 3: = 0.6020 + 0.4771 − 1 = **0.0791**.

**Example 2.** Solve log(x + 3) + log(x − 3) = log 16.
Step 1: Combine: log[(x + 3)(x − 3)] = log 16.
Step 2: x² − 9 = 16, so x² = 25, x = ±5.
Step 3: x − 3 must be positive, so reject −5. **x = 5**.

Always check that every log argument stays positive at the end.

To find log 346.7 with tables: write it as 3.467 × 10². The **characteristic** is 2; look up the mantissa of 3467 in the table (about .5400). So log 346.7 ≈ 2.5400. For 0.003467 the mantissa is the same but the characteristic is 3̄, written 3̄.5400 (meaning −3 + 0.5400).

**Antilog** reverses this: antilog of 2.5400 ≈ 346.7. Tables let you multiply big numbers by adding logs — the historical reason logs were invented.

log(m + n) is **not** log m + log n, and log m / log n is **not** log(m/n). The mantissa is always taken as positive; that is why a negative characteristic is written with a bar instead of mixing signs.

**Example 3.** If log 2 = 0.3010, how many digits does 8¹⁰ have?
Step 1: log 8¹⁰ = 30 log 2 = 9.030.
Step 2: Characteristic 9, so the number has **10 digits**.

Also watch the base: log₂ 8 = 3 but log 8 (base 10) ≈ 0.903. When a question mixes bases, convert everything with the change-of-base rule before simplifying.
Formulas for log questions.
points: log mn = log m + log n
log m/n = log m − log n
log_a b = log b / log a

cards.title: Ratio basics
cards.body: A **ratio** a : b compares two like quantities (same units) and equals a/b. It is unchanged when both terms are multiplied or divided by the same non-zero number. Combined ratio: if a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, scale b to 12 → a : b : c = 8 : 12 : 15.

cards.title: Proportion
points: a : b = c : d ⇔ ad = bc
Fourth proportional to a, b, c = bc/a
Third proportional to a, b = b²/a

cards.title: Variation
cards.body: **Direct**: y ∝ x ⇒ y = kx (ratio constant). **Inverse**: y ∝ 1/x ⇒ xy = k (product constant). **Joint**: y ∝ xz ⇒ y = kxz. Find k from one set of values, then substitute.

cards.title: Unitary method
cards.body: Find the value of **one unit**, then multiply. More men → fewer days (inverse); more articles → more cost (direct). The chain rule: M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂.

cards.title: Dividing in a ratio
cards.body: Divide ₹1,800 among A, B, C in ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Total parts 9; one part = ₹200. Shares **₹400, ₹600, ₹800**.

cards.title: Partnership
cards.body: Profit is shared in the ratio **capital × time**. A invests ₹5,000 for 12 months, B ₹6,000 for 8 months → 60,000 : 48,000 = **5 : 4**.

cards.q: The mean proportional between 4 and 25 is:
If x varies inversely as y and x = 6 when y = 4, find x when y = 8.
If a : b = 3 : 4 and b : c = 6 : 7, then a : c is:

notes.p:
A ratio compares quantities of the same kind; convert units first (40 cm : 2 m = 40 : 200 = 1 : 5). **Duplicate ratio** of a : b is a² : b²; **sub-duplicate** is √a : √b; **triplicate** a³ : b³.

If a number x is added to both terms to make a new ratio, set up an equation. **Example 1.** What must be added to each of 5 and 9 to make the ratio 3 : 4?
Step 1: (5 + x)/(9 + x) = 3/4.
Step 2: 20 + 4x = 27 + 3x.
Step 3: **x = 7** (check 12 : 16 = 3 : 4).
points: a : b = ka : kb for k ≠ 0

notes.p:
Four numbers are in **proportion** if a : b = c : d, i.e. product of extremes = product of means (ad = bc). The properties **invertendo, alternendo, componendo, dividendo** and **componendo-dividendo** let you rearrange quickly.

**Example 2.** If (x + y)/(x − y) = 7/3, find x : y.
Step 1: Componendo-dividendo: x/y = (7 + 3)/(7 − 3) = 10/4.
Step 2: **x : y = 5 : 2**.

The CDS syllabus lists **variation** separately. In direct variation, doubling x doubles y; in inverse variation, doubling x halves y.

**Example 3.** The area of a circle varies directly as the square of its radius. If radius increases by 20%, area increases by?
Step 1: A = kr². New r = 1.2r.
Step 2: New A = k(1.44r²).
Step 3: Increase = **44%**.

**Example 4.** 12 men build a wall in 10 days. How many days for 15 men? Men × days constant: 120 = 15 × d, so **d = 8**.

Mixtures are ratio problems. **Alligation**: when two items at prices c₁ (cheaper) and c₂ (dearer) give a mean m, quantity ratio = (c₂ − m) : (m − c₁).

In **partnership**, profit ratio = (capital × months). If one partner is a working partner with a salary, pay that first, then split the rest.

**Example 5.** In what ratio must rice at ₹40/kg be mixed with rice at ₹55/kg to get a mixture worth ₹45/kg?
Step 1: Cheaper c₁ = 40, dearer c₂ = 55, mean m = 45.
Step 2: Ratio = (55 − 45) : (45 − 40) = 10 : 5.
Step 3: **2 : 1** (cheaper : dearer).

A ratio of 2 : 3 does not mean the quantities are 2 and 3 — they are 2k and 3k. In "x added to both" problems never add x to only one term. In inverse variation, check whether the problem has a third quantity (hours per day) hidden in it.
Ratio and variation summary.
points: Direct: y = kx; inverse: xy = k

cards.title: Percentage change
points: Successive a% and b%: net = a + b + ab/100
Price up r% → consumption cut r/(100 + r) × 100 to keep spend same
A is r% more than B → B is r/(100 + r) × 100 less than A

cards.title: Profit, loss, discount
points: Discount is on marked price (MP): SP = MP(100 − D%)/100
Two discounts d₁, d₂ = d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100

cards.title: Marked price
cards.body: CP ₹800. Shopkeeper wants 20% profit after a 20% discount. SP = 960. MP × 0.8 = 960 → **MP = ₹1,200**, i.e. marked 50% above CP.

cards.title: False weights
cards.body: A trader uses 900 g for 1 kg and sells at CP. Gain = 100/900 × 100 = **11.11%** (error over the true weight given).

cards.title: Same SP, same %
cards.body: If two articles are sold at the same SP, one at x% gain and the other at x% loss, there is always a **loss of x²/100 %**. For x = 10: loss 1%.

cards.q: A number is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. Net change:
An article is sold at ₹540 at a loss of 10%. Its cost price is:
Two successive discounts of 10% and 20% are equal to a single discount of:

notes.p:
A percentage is always "of something". When A is 25% more than B, B is 25/125 = **20%** less than A, because the base has changed. Converting percentages to fractions (25% = 1/4) makes most calculations a one-step job.

**Example 1.** In an election between two candidates, the winner gets 58% of valid votes and wins by 2,560 votes. Total valid votes?
Step 1: Loser gets 42%; margin = 16%.
Step 2: 16% of V = 2,560 → V = **16,000**.
points: x% of y = y% of x
Population after n years = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ

notes.p:
Two successive changes of a% and b% give **a + b + ab/100** (use negative signs for decreases). This one formula covers price-quantity problems, successive discounts, and area changes.

**Example 2.** Length of a rectangle rises 10%, breadth falls 10%. Area change?
Step 1: a = 10, b = −10.
Step 2: 10 − 10 − 100/100 = **−1%** (1% decrease).

Profit and loss % are calculated on **cost price** unless the question says otherwise. When overheads (transport, repairs) are paid, add them to CP.

**Example 3.** A man buys a scooter for ₹40,000, spends ₹5,000 on repairs and sells it for ₹49,500. Profit %?
Step 1: Effective CP = 45,000.
Step 2: Profit = 4,500.
Step 3: % = 4,500/45,000 × 100 = **10%**.

**Example 5.** By selling an article for ₹1,035 a man gains 15%. What should he sell it for to gain 25%?
Step 1: CP = 1,035 × 100/115 = ₹900.
Step 2: New SP = 900 × 125/100 = **₹1,125**.
Shortcut: new SP = old SP × 125/115 directly, without finding CP.

Discount is always on the **marked (list) price**. The relation that joins everything is **MP × (100 − D)/100 = CP × (100 + P)/100**.

**Example 4.** A trader marks goods 40% above CP and gives 15% discount. Profit %?
Step 1: Take CP = 100, MP = 140.
Step 2: SP = 140 × 0.85 = 119.
Step 3: Profit = **19%**.

"Buy 4 get 1 free" is a discount of 1/5 = 20%, not 25%.

Calculating profit on SP instead of CP; adding successive percentages directly; treating "buy 2 get 1 free" as 50% off (it is 33⅓%); and forgetting that a fixed percentage increase followed by the same decrease always gives a net **loss**.

A useful habit: assume CP = 100 (or MP = 100) whenever no actual amount is given. Percentages then become plain numbers and the answer falls out without algebra. Check the final answer against the options by reverse calculation — it takes ten seconds and catches most base errors.
Formulas to keep handy.

cards.title: Simple interest
points: Sum doubles in T years at SI → R = 100/T
Equal SI on different principals: P₁R₁T₁ = P₂R₂T₂

cards.title: CI − SI shortcuts
points: Different rates: A = P(1 + R₁/100)(1 + R₂/100)…

cards.title: Effective rate
cards.body: At 10% CI, two years give 21% (10 + 10 + 100/100) — the successive-percentage formula. Three years give 33.1%. Use this to answer many CI questions without powers.

cards.title: Doubling
cards.body: A sum doubles in 5 years at CI. In how many years will it become 8 times? 8 = 2³, so **15 years**.

cards.title: Instalments
cards.body: For equal annual instalments x under CI at R%: P = x/(1 + R/100) + x/(1 + R/100)² + … (each instalment discounted back to today).

cards.q: SI on ₹5,000 at 8% p.a. for 3 years is:
Difference between CI and SI on ₹8,000 for 2 years at 5% is:
At what SI rate does a sum double in 8 years?

notes.p:
Simple interest is charged only on the **original principal**, so interest is the same every year. SI = PRT/100; time must be in years (months ÷ 12) and rate per annum.

**Example 1.** A sum amounts to ₹7,200 in 2 years and ₹8,400 in 4 years at SI. Find P and R.
Step 1: 2 years of interest = 8,400 − 7,200 = 1,200 → ₹600 per year.
Step 2: P = 7,200 − 2 × 600 = **₹6,000**.
Step 3: R = 600/6,000 × 100 = **10%**.
points: Same sum, same rate: SI ∝ time

notes.p:
In compound interest, interest is added to the principal at the end of each period, so the next period earns interest on interest. **A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ**.

**Example 2.** ₹16,000 at 10% p.a. compounded half-yearly for 1 year.
Step 1: Rate per half-year = 5%, periods = 2.
Step 2: A = 16,000 × 1.05 × 1.05 = 16,000 × 1.1025 = 17,640.
Step 3: CI = **₹1,640** (yearly compounding would give ₹1,600).

The difference arises only from interest on interest. For 2 years: **D = P(R/100)²**. For 3 years: **D = P(R/100)²(3 + R/100)**.

**Example 3.** CI − SI for 2 years at 10% is ₹50. Find P.
Step 1: P × (0.1)² = 50.
Step 2: P = 50/0.01 = **₹5,000**.

The CI formula models population growth and machine depreciation. Population of 50,000 growing 4% a year becomes 50,000 × 1.04² = **54,080** in 2 years. A machine worth ₹1,00,000 depreciating 10% a year is worth 1,00,000 × 0.9² = ₹81,000 after 2 years.

If a sum becomes k times in n years at CI, it becomes kᵐ times in mn years.

**Example 4.** A sum of ₹2,100 is lent at 10% CI, to be repaid in two equal annual instalments. Find each instalment.
Step 1: Present value of instalment x after 1 year = x/1.1 and after 2 years = x/1.21.
Step 2: x/1.1 + x/1.21 = 2,100 → x(1.1 + 1)/1.21 = 2,100.
Step 3: x = 2,100 × 1.21/2.1 = **₹1,210**.

Forgetting to halve the rate and double the periods for half-yearly compounding; computing CI and stopping at the amount; and using SI doubling logic (which is linear) for CI (which is exponential: a sum that doubles in 5 years quadruples in 10, not 15).

Also watch the wording "rate of interest per annum, compounded annually" versus "simple interest for the first year, compound thereafter": for one year, SI and CI (compounded yearly) are equal. Questions that give CI for year 1 and year 2 separately reveal the rate directly: R = (I₂ − I₁)/I₁ × 100.
Interest formulas.
points: Doubles at SI in T years → R = 100/T
k times in n yrs (CI) → kᵐ in mn yrs

cards.title: Work as rate
cards.body: If A does a job in a days, A does **1/a** of it per day. Rates add when people work together. Total work = rate × time.

cards.title: Core formulas
points: A and B together: ab/(a + b) days
If A is k times as efficient as B, A takes 1/k of B's time

cards.title: LCM method
cards.body: Take total work = LCM of the days. A: 12 days, B: 18 days → work 36 units; A does 3 units/day, B 2 units/day; together 5 units/day → **7.2 days**. Avoids fractions.

cards.title: Pipes and cisterns
cards.body: Inlet pipes add rate; outlet (leak) pipes subtract rate. A fills in a hours, B empties in b hours → net fill time = ab/(b − a) (b > a).

cards.title: Work and wages
cards.body: A and B do a job for ₹1,500. A alone 10 days, B 15 days. Wages are in ratio of work done = rates 1/10 : 1/15 = 3 : 2 → A gets **₹900**, B ₹600.

cards.title: Leaving midway
cards.body: If someone leaves before the end, count each person's days separately: work = Σ (rate × days worked) = 1.

cards.q: A can do a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. Together they need:
A pipe fills a tank in 6 h and a leak empties it in 12 h. With both, the tank fills in:
15 men finish a work in 20 days. In how many days will 25 men finish it?

notes.p:
Time-and-work is part of the **unitary method** in the CDS syllabus. Convert everyone into a **rate** (job per day). Rates add for people working together; a leak or a destructive worker has a negative rate.

Because work done = rate × time, the person with the higher **efficiency** takes less time: time is inversely proportional to efficiency.
points: Efficiency ratio = inverse of time ratio
Wages are shared in proportion to work done
Use LCM of days as "total units" to avoid fractions

notes.p:
**Example 1.** A and B can do a job in 12 days, B and C in 15 days, C and A in 20 days. How long for all three? How long for A alone?
Step 1: Take work = LCM(12, 15, 20) = 60 units.
Step 2: A+B = 5, B+C = 4, C+A = 3 units/day. Adding: 2(A+B+C) = 12, so A+B+C = 6 units/day.
Step 3: All three: 60/6 = **10 days**.
Step 4: A = 6 − (B+C) = 2 units/day → **30 days** alone.

**Example 2.** A can do a job in 10 days and B in 15 days. They start together, but A leaves after 3 days. How many more days does B take?
Step 1: Work = 30 units; A = 3, B = 2 units/day.
Step 2: In 3 days together: 3 × 5 = 15 units.
Step 3: Remaining 15 units at 2/day = **7.5 days**.

**Example 4.** A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish a job in 18 days. How long would A alone take?
Step 1: Let B do 1 unit/day; A does 2 units/day; together 3 units/day.
Step 2: Total work = 3 × 18 = 54 units.
Step 3: A alone = 54/2 = **27 days** (B alone would take 54 days).

Treat filling as positive work and emptying as negative work. **Example 3.** Pipes A and B fill a tank in 10 h and 15 h; pipe C empties it in 30 h. All open: rates 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 units/h on 30 units → **7.5 h**.

For man-days questions with hours per day or different amounts of work, use **M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂**.

Adding days instead of rates (A 10 days + B 15 days is not 25 days together); forgetting that a leak subtracts; splitting wages by days instead of by work done; and mixing hours with days in the chain formula.

Check your answer for reasonableness: two people together must finish faster than the quicker one alone, but never in less than half of the quicker one's time. If your "together" answer exceeds the faster person's time, you have added times instead of rates.

In pipe problems, a tank that is "half full" needs only half the work; read the starting level carefully.
Time and work at a glance.

cards.title: Relative speed
points: Train crosses a pole: time = train length/speed
Train crosses platform/train: (sum of lengths)/relative speed

cards.title: Boats and streams
points: Downstream = b + s; upstream = b − s

cards.title: Train and platform
cards.body: A 200 m train at 72 km/h crosses a 300 m platform. Speed = 20 m/s; distance = 500 m; time = **25 s**.

cards.title: Late and early
cards.body: Walking at 5 km/h a boy is 7 min late; at 6 km/h he is 5 min early. Time gap 12 min = 1/5 h. d/5 − d/6 = 1/5 → d/30 = 1/5 → **d = 6 km**.

cards.title: Ratio thinking
cards.body: For a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional. If speed becomes 4/5, time becomes 5/4 — an increase of one-quarter of the usual time.

cards.q: A car goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed:
Two trains 150 m and 100 m long run in opposite directions at 40 km/h and 50 km/h. Time to cross each other:
A boat goes 12 km/h downstream and 8 km/h upstream. Speed of the stream:

notes.p:
Everything follows from **d = s × t**. Keep units consistent: convert km/h to m/s with **5/18** whenever lengths are in metres and time in seconds.

Average speed is **total distance ÷ total time**, never the simple average of speeds unless the times are equal. For equal distances at x and y, it is the harmonic mean 2xy/(x + y).

Two bodies moving the same way close the gap at the **difference** of speeds; opposite ways, at the **sum**. A train is a moving body with length: to pass a pole or man it covers its own length; to pass a platform, bridge or another train it covers both lengths.

**Example 1.** A train passes a pole in 15 s and a 100 m platform in 25 s. Find its length and speed.
Step 1: Let length L, speed v. L = 15v and L + 100 = 25v.
Step 2: Subtract: 100 = 10v → v = 10 m/s = **36 km/h**.
Step 3: L = **150 m**.

Downstream the stream helps (b + s); upstream it opposes (b − s).

**Example 2.** A boat covers 24 km upstream and 36 km downstream in 6 h, and 36 km upstream and 24 km downstream in 6.5 h. Find the speeds.
Step 1: Let 1/u = x, 1/d = y. 24x + 36y = 6 and 36x + 24y = 6.5.
Step 2: Adding: 60(x + y) = 12.5; subtracting: 12(x − y) = 0.5.
Step 3: x + y = 5/24, x − y = 1/24 → x = 1/8, y = 1/12. So u = 8, d = 12 km/h.
Step 4: Boat = **10 km/h**, stream = **2 km/h**.

When two people start towards each other d km apart, they meet after d/(sum of speeds). When one chases another who has a head start of d km, catching up takes d/(difference of speeds). Circular tracks: runners meet at the start again after the LCM of their lap times.

**Example 3.** A thief runs at 8 km/h. A policeman starts chasing 10 minutes later at 10 km/h. When does he catch the thief?
Step 1: Head start = 8 × 10/60 = 4/3 km.
Step 2: Relative speed = 2 km/h.
Step 3: Time = (4/3)/2 = 2/3 h = **40 minutes** after the policeman starts.
Not converting units; forgetting the train's own length; averaging speeds directly; and adding the stream speed upstream. Read whether time is given in minutes and convert before solving.
Distance formulas.
points: Same direction: s₁ − s₂; opposite: s₁ + s₂
Down = b + s; up = b − s

chapters.title: Maths: polynomials, remainder theorem & rational expressions

cards.title: Polynomial basics
cards.body: A **polynomial** in x has whole-number powers only. Its **degree** is the highest power. Linear: degree 1; quadratic: 2; cubic: 3. √x or 1/x terms mean it is not a polynomial.

cards.title: Remainder and factor theorems
cards.body: When p(x) is divided by (x − a), the **remainder is p(a)**. If p(a) = 0, then **(x − a) is a factor**. For division by (ax − b), remainder = p(b/a).

cards.title: Key identities
points: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca)
If a + b + c = 0, a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

cards.title: HCF and LCM of polynomials
cards.body: Factorise fully. **HCF** = product of common factors with lowest powers; **LCM** = all factors with highest powers. For two polynomials, HCF × LCM = product of the polynomials (up to a constant).

cards.title: Remainder theorem
cards.body: Remainder when x³ − 2x² + 4x − 5 is divided by (x − 2): p(2) = 8 − 8 + 8 − 5 = **3**.

cards.title: Conditional identities
cards.body: When a condition is given (like a + b + c = 0 or x + 1/x = 3), use it to substitute rather than solving for each variable. If x + 1/x = 3, then x² + 1/x² = 9 − 2 = **7**.

cards.q: If (x − 1) is a factor of x³ + kx² − 4x + 2, then k is:
If a + b + c = 0, then (a³ + b³ + c³)/abc equals:
cards.explain: a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc when a + b + c = 0.

cards.q: If x + 1/x = 4, x² + 1/x² is:

notes.p:
The CDS algebra syllabus begins with **basic operations** (adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing algebraic expressions) and **simple factors**. Factorise by taking common factors, grouping, using identities, or splitting the middle term.

Examples of factorising:
• 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)
• x² − 9y² = (x − 3y)(x + 3y)
• ax + ay + bx + by = (a + b)(x + y)
• x³ − 27 = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9)
points: Degree of a product = sum of degrees
A non-zero constant is a polynomial of degree 0
Coefficients can be any real numbers

notes.p:
Dividing p(x) by (x − a) gives p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. Put x = a: **r = p(a)**. This saves long division.

**Example 1.** Find k if x³ − 3x² + kx − 6 leaves remainder 4 when divided by (x − 2).
Step 1: p(2) = 8 − 12 + 2k − 6 = 2k − 10.
Step 2: 2k − 10 = 4 → **k = 7**.

**Example 2.** Factorise x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.
Step 1: Try x = 1: 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor.
Step 2: Divide: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3).
Step 3: **(x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3)**.

Tip: try factors of the constant term (±1, ±2, ±3 …) as roots.

**Example 3.** HCF and LCM of x² − 4 and x² + x − 6.
Step 1: x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2); x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2).
Step 2: HCF = **(x − 2)**.
Step 3: LCM = **(x − 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)**.

The syllabus asks for HCF and LCM of polynomials in the same spirit as for numbers — factorise into "prime" (irreducible) factors first.

A **rational expression** is a ratio of polynomials, p(x)/q(x) with q(x) ≠ 0. Simplify by factorising top and bottom and cancelling common factors; add by taking the LCM of the denominators.

**Example 4.** Simplify (x² − 1)/(x² + 2x + 1).
Step 1: = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x + 1)².
Step 2: = **(x − 1)/(x + 1)**, for x ≠ −1.

These hold only under a stated condition. The most-tested ones:
• If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
• If x + 1/x = k, then x² + 1/x² = k² − 2 and x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k.
• If x − 1/x = k, then x² + 1/x² = k² + 2.

**Example 5.** If x + 1/x = 3, find x³ + 1/x³: 27 − 9 = **18**.

A fast check for any identity question is to plug in small numbers (a = 1, b = −1, c = 0) and test the options.
Algebra essentials.
points: a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc if a + b + c = 0

chapters.title: Maths: quadratic equations & nature of roots

cards.title: Standard form
cards.body: A quadratic equation is **ax² + bx + c = 0**, a ≠ 0. It has at most two roots. Solve by factorising, completing the square, or the formula.

cards.title: Quadratic formula and discriminant
points: D < 0: no real roots (CDS considers real roots only)

cards.title: Roots and coefficients
points: Equation with roots α, β: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0

cards.title: Splitting the middle term
cards.body: x² − 7x + 12 = 0: find two numbers with product 12 and sum −7 → −3, −4. (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0 → **x = 3 or 4**.

cards.title: Forming an equation
cards.body: Roots 2 and −5: sum −3, product −10. Equation: **x² + 3x − 10 = 0**.

cards.title: Word problems
cards.body: Translate to one equation in one unknown, solve, then reject roots that make no physical sense (negative lengths, fractional people).

cards.q: Sum of roots of 2x² − 8x + 3 = 0 is:
For what value of k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have equal roots?
If α, β are roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0, α² + β² equals:

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus covers **solutions of quadratic equations** and the **relation between roots and coefficients**, considering only real roots.

**Factorisation** is fastest when it works: for ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is ac and whose sum is b.

**Example 1.** Solve 6x² − x − 2 = 0.
Step 1: ac = −12; numbers with product −12 and sum −1: −4 and 3.
Step 2: 6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = 2x(3x − 2) + 1(3x − 2) = (2x + 1)(3x − 2).
Step 3: **x = −1/2 or 2/3**.
points: Always bring the equation to standard form first
Divide through by a common factor

notes.h: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
notes.p:
When factorising is hard, use x = [−b ± √D]/2a with **D = b² − 4ac**.

**Example 2.** Solve x² − 4x + 1 = 0.
Step 1: D = 16 − 4 = 12.
Step 2: x = (4 ± √12)/2 = (4 ± 2√3)/2.
Step 3: **x = 2 ± √3**.

The discriminant tells you the nature of roots without solving. If a, b, c are rational and D is a perfect square, the roots are rational. Irrational roots come in conjugate pairs (2 + √3 and 2 − √3).

For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β: **α + β = −b/a**, **αβ = c/a**. Many CDS questions ask for symmetric expressions of the roots without solving.

**Example 3.** If α, β are roots of x² − 6x + 4 = 0, find 1/α + 1/β and α³ + β³.
Step 1: α + β = 6, αβ = 4.
Step 2: 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ = 6/4 = **3/2**.
Step 3: α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β) = 216 − 72 = **144**.

The syllabus mentions **practical problems leading to quadratic equations in one variable**.

**Example 4.** The product of two consecutive positive integers is 132. Find them.
Step 1: x(x + 1) = 132 → x² + x − 132 = 0.
Step 2: (x + 12)(x − 11) = 0.
Step 3: x = 11 (reject −12). Integers: **11 and 12**.

**Example 5.** A rectangle has perimeter 34 m and area 60 m². Sides: l + b = 17, lb = 60 → l, b are roots of t² − 17t + 60 = 0 → **12 m and 5 m**.

Dividing both sides by x (loses the root x = 0); forgetting the sign in −b/a; and not rejecting impossible roots in word problems. If one root is given, substitute it to find an unknown coefficient, then use sum or product to find the other root.
Quadratic summary.
points: D > 0, = 0, < 0 → distinct, equal, no real roots
x² − Sx + P = 0 from sum S, product P
Never divide by a variable that may be 0

chapters.title: Maths: linear equations & inequations in two variables

cards.title: Two equations, two unknowns
cards.body: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ represent two straight lines. Their intersection point is the solution. Solve by **substitution**, **elimination** or **cross-multiplication**.

cards.title: Consistency conditions
points: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂: infinitely many (same line)

cards.title: Graphical solution
cards.body: Plot each line using two points (intercepts are easiest: put x = 0, then y = 0). Read the intersection point. Parallel lines never meet; coincident lines overlap.

cards.title: Linear inequations
cards.body: ax + by ≤ c describes a **half-plane**. Draw the line ax + by = c (solid for ≤/≥, dashed for </>), test the origin, and shade the side that satisfies it. A system's solution is the overlap of the shaded regions.

cards.title: Inequality signs
cards.body: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a **negative** number reverses the sign: −2x > 6 ⇒ x < −3.

cards.q: For what k do 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + ky = 10 have infinitely many solutions?
Which point satisfies x + y ≤ 4 and x ≥ 1?
The lines 3x − y = 2 and 6x − 2y = 7 are:

notes.p:
The syllabus names **simultaneous linear equations in two unknowns — analytical and graphical solutions**. Analytical methods:
• **Substitution**: express one variable from one equation and substitute.
• **Elimination**: multiply to match coefficients, then add or subtract.
• **Cross-multiplication**: x/(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁) = y/(c₁a₂ − c₂a₁) = 1/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) for equations written as a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0.

**Example 1.** Solve 3x + 2y = 12 and 5x − 3y = 1.
Step 1: Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: 9x + 6y = 36, 10x − 6y = 2.
Step 2: Add: 19x = 38 → x = 2.
Step 3: y = (12 − 6)/2 = 3. **(2, 3)**.
points: Check the answer in both equations
Look for symmetric equations: add and subtract them

notes.p:
Each equation is a line. **Intersecting** lines give exactly one solution (consistent); **parallel** lines none (inconsistent); **coincident** lines infinitely many (dependent). The ratio test on coefficients tells you which, without drawing.

When drawing, find two or three points per line, e.g. for x + y = 5: (0, 5), (5, 0), (2, 3). The area of the triangle formed by two lines and an axis is a common follow-up question: find the vertices and use ½ × base × height.

**Example 2.** Five years ago, a father was seven times as old as his son. Five years hence, he will be three times as old. Find present ages.
Step 1: Let ages be F and S. F − 5 = 7(S − 5) → F = 7S − 30.
Step 2: F + 5 = 3(S + 5) → F = 3S + 10.
Step 3: 7S − 30 = 3S + 10 → S = 10, F = 40. Father **40**, son **10**.

**Example 3.** A two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits. If 18 is added to it, the digits are reversed. Find the number.
Step 1: Let the number be 10a + b. Then 10a + b = 4(a + b) → 6a = 3b → b = 2a.
Step 2: 10a + b + 18 = 10b + a → 9(b − a) = 18 → b − a = 2.
Step 3: a = 2, b = 4. The number is **24** (check: 4 × 6 = 24 and 24 + 18 = 42).

To solve a system like x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0:
Step 1: Draw x + 2y = 8 through (8, 0) and (0, 4).
Step 2: Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 8 true, so shade the side containing the origin.
Step 3: x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 restrict to the first quadrant.
The solution region is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (8, 0), (0, 4).

If the line passes through the origin, test another point such as (1, 0).

Forgetting to reverse the inequality when multiplying by a negative; using a solid line for a strict inequality; and mis-reading the consistency ratios (c₁/c₂ matters only when the a and b ratios are equal).
Linear equations at a glance.

chapters.title: Maths: set language & laws of indices

cards.title: Set notation
cards.body: A **set** is a well-defined collection. ∈ means "belongs to"; ⊂ "is a subset of"; ∅ is the empty set; U is the universal set. A set with n elements has **2ⁿ subsets**.

cards.title: Set operations
points: A ∪ B: in A or B; A ∩ B: in both
A − B: in A but not B
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
De Morgan: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′; (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′

cards.title: Venn diagram
cards.body: In a class of 50, 30 play cricket, 25 play football and 10 play both. Number playing at least one = 30 + 25 − 10 = 45; neither = **5**.

cards.title: Equating powers
cards.body: If aˣ = aʸ (a > 0, a ≠ 1) then x = y. Write both sides with the same base: 4ˣ = 32 → 2²ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5/2.

cards.q: Number of subsets of {a, b, c, d}:
If 3ˣ⁺¹ = 81, x equals:

notes.p:
The syllabus includes **set language and set notation**. Sets are written in roster form {2, 4, 6} or set-builder form {x : x is an even number < 8}. Two sets are **equal** if they have exactly the same elements; **equivalent** if they have the same number of elements.

Key kinds: **empty set** ∅ (no elements), **singleton** (one element), **finite/infinite**, **subset** (every element of A is in B), **proper subset**, **power set** P(A) (set of all subsets, size 2ⁿ), and **disjoint sets** (A ∩ B = ∅).
points: ∅ is a subset of every set
Every set is a subset of itself
Proper subsets of an n-element set: 2ⁿ − 1

notes.p:
Union, intersection, difference and complement are best seen on a **Venn diagram**. For counting, use **n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)** and, for three sets, n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A∩B) − n(B∩C) − n(C∩A) + n(A∩B∩C).

**Example 1.** In a survey of 100 people, 60 read newspaper A, 50 read B and 20 read both. How many read only A? How many read neither?
Step 1: Only A = 60 − 20 = **40**.
Step 2: At least one = 60 + 50 − 20 = 90.
Step 3: Neither = 100 − 90 = **10**.

All index laws come from counting factors: a³ × a² = (a·a·a)(a·a) = a⁵. Negative indices mean reciprocals; fractional indices mean roots.

**Example 2.** Simplify (2⁵ × 8²)/(4³).
Step 1: Convert to base 2: 8² = 2⁶, 4³ = 2⁶.
Step 2: 2⁵ × 2⁶ ÷ 2⁶ = **2⁵ = 32**.

**Example 3.** Solve 2ˣ × 4ˣ = 512.
Step 1: 2ˣ × 2²ˣ = 2³ˣ.
Step 2: 512 = 2⁹, so 3x = 9 → **x = 3**.

To compare 2³⁰, 3²⁰ and 5¹⁰, reduce to a common exponent of 10: (2³)¹⁰ = 8¹⁰, (3²)¹⁰ = 9¹⁰, 5¹⁰. So 3²⁰ is the largest and 5¹⁰ the smallest.

Also useful: (a/b)⁻ⁿ = (b/a)ⁿ, and √a × ∛a = a^(1/2 + 1/3) = a^(5/6).

**Example 4.** Find x if (√3)ˣ = 81.
Step 1: (√3)ˣ = 3^(x/2).
Step 2: 81 = 3⁴, so x/2 = 4.
Step 3: **x = 8**.

Whenever the bases are different (4, 8, 16, 32), rewrite everything in the smallest prime base before applying any law.

a⁰ = 1 only for a ≠ 0; (a + b)ⁿ is not aⁿ + bⁿ; (−8)^(1/3) = −2 is fine but even roots of negatives are not real. In sets, forgetting to subtract the intersection double-counts; "only A" excludes the overlap.
Sets and indices.
points: Compare powers by a common exponent

cards.title: Ratios in a right triangle
cards.body: For an acute angle θ: **sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse**, **cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse**, **tan θ = opposite/adjacent**. cosec, sec, cot are the reciprocals. Memory aid: SOH-CAH-TOA.

cards.title: Standard values
points: sin θ = cos(90° − θ); tan θ = cot(90° − θ)

cards.title: Identities
points: sec θ − tan θ = 1/(sec θ + tan θ)

cards.title: Finding other ratios
cards.body: If sin θ = 3/5 (θ acute), the triangle is 3-4-5: cos θ = **4/5**, tan θ = **3/4**.

cards.title: Trend check
cards.body: From 0° to 90°, sin and tan **increase**, cos **decreases**. So sin 50° > sin 40°, and cos 50° < cos 40°. Use this to eliminate options and read tables sensibly.

cards.q: sin 30° × cos 60° + cos 30° × sin 60° equals:
If tan θ = 1 (0° < θ < 90°), sin θ + cos θ =
(1 − sin²θ) sec²θ equals:

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus restricts trigonometry to **sin x, cos x, tan x for 0° < x < 90°**, values at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, **simple identities**, **use of trigonometric tables**, and **heights and distances**.

All six ratios come from one right triangle. Once you know one ratio, draw the triangle, find the third side by Pythagoras, and read off the rest.
points: sin and cos are never more than 1 for acute angles
tan can be any positive value

notes.p:
Learn the sin row as √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2 for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°; the cos row is the same in reverse; tan = sin/cos.

**Example 1.** Evaluate (4 sin²60° + 3 tan²30° − 8 sin 45° cos 45°).
Step 1: sin²60° = 3/4 → 4 × 3/4 = 3.
Step 2: tan²30° = 1/3 → 3 × 1/3 = 1.
Step 3: sin 45° cos 45° = 1/2 → 8 × 1/2 = 4.
Step 4: 3 + 1 − 4 = **0**.

Three Pythagorean identities do most of the work. To prove or simplify, convert everything to sin and cos, or multiply by a conjugate.

**Example 2.** If sec θ + tan θ = 2, find sec θ − tan θ and sin θ.
Step 1: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, so sec θ − tan θ = **1/2**.
Step 2: Adding: 2 sec θ = 5/2 → sec θ = 5/4; subtracting: 2 tan θ = 3/2 → tan θ = 3/4.
Step 3: sin θ = tan θ/sec θ = (3/4)/(5/4) = **3/5**.

**Example 3.** Simplify (sin θ + cos θ)² + (sin θ − cos θ)² = 2(sin²θ + cos²θ) = **2**.

sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ. Products like tan 1° tan 2° … tan 89° pair up (tan θ × cot θ = 1) and equal **1**, because tan 45° = 1 sits in the middle.

If sin A = cos B for acute A and B, then **A + B = 90°**.

Tables list sin, cos and tan for angles in degrees and minutes (usually with mean-difference columns). To read sin 37°24′, find the row 37° and the column nearest 24′, then add the mean difference for the extra minutes. For **cos**, the mean difference is **subtracted**, because cos decreases as the angle increases. In the exam, values such as sin 37° ≈ 0.6 and tan 37° ≈ 0.75 are sometimes given — use them as supplied.
Trigonometry checklist.
points: sin, tan ↑ and cos ↓ from 0° to 90°
Subtract mean difference for cos in tables

cards.title: Angles of elevation and depression
cards.body: The **angle of elevation** is measured upward from the horizontal to the object; the **angle of depression** is downward from the horizontal to the object. Angle of depression from A to B = angle of elevation from B to A (alternate angles).

cards.title: One angle
cards.body: A tower casts a shadow 20 m long when the sun's elevation is 60°. Height = 20 tan 60° = **20√3 m** ≈ 34.64 m.

cards.title: Two angles
cards.body: From two points on the same side, 20 m apart, the elevations of a tower top are 30° and 60°. Then h = d√3 and h = (d + 20)/√3 → 3d = d + 20 → d = 10, **h = 10√3 m**.

cards.title: Standard results
cards.body: For elevations 30° and 60° from two points on the same side a distance a apart, height = **a√3/2**. If the shadow at 30° is longer than at 60° by a, the same formula applies.

cards.title: Draw first
cards.body: Always draw a neat right triangle, mark the right angle, the known side and the angle. Use tan for height-distance pairs; use sin or cos only when a slanting length (ladder, string) is involved.

cards.q: A ladder 10 m long makes 60° with the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
The angle of elevation of the top of a 50 m tower from a point is 45°. Distance of the point from the foot:
From the top of a 30 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 30°. Distance of the boat from the cliff foot:

notes.p:
**Heights and distances** applies trigonometry to real objects: towers, poles, kites, aeroplanes and ships. The CDS syllabus calls these "simple cases", so almost every question uses 30°, 45° or 60° and a single right triangle or two triangles that share a side.

The observer's eye is assumed to be at ground level unless a height is given, and the ground is horizontal.
points: Depression: look down; equals elevation from the other end
Shadow length is the horizontal side

notes.p:
**Example 1.** A kite is flying on a string 100 m long, inclined at 30° to the ground. Height of the kite?
Step 1: The string is the hypotenuse; we want the opposite side.
Step 2: h = 100 sin 30° = 100 × 1/2 = **50 m**.

**Example 2.** From a point 30 m from the foot of a pole, the elevation of its top is 30°. Height = 30 tan 30° = 30/√3 = **10√3 m** ≈ 17.32 m.

When two angles are given, write two equations with the common side and solve.

**Example 3.** From the top of a 60 m building, the angles of depression of the top and bottom of a tower are 30° and 60°. Find the tower's height.
Step 1: Horizontal distance d: tan 60° = 60/d → d = 60/√3 = 20√3 m.
Step 2: Vertical drop to the tower top: d tan 30° = 20√3 × 1/√3 = 20 m.
Step 3: Tower height = 60 − 20 = **40 m**.

**Example 4.** An aeroplane at 3,000 m height is seen at elevation 60°, and after 15 s at 30°. Its speed?
Step 1: Horizontal distances: 3,000/√3 = 1,000√3 and 3,000√3.
Step 2: Distance flown = 2,000√3 m ≈ 3,464 m.
Step 3: Speed = 2,000√3/15 ≈ **231 m/s**.

If the angles of elevation from two points at distances a and b from the foot (same side, same line) are complementary, the height is **√(ab)**. For example, distances 4 m and 9 m with complementary elevations give height 6 m. Proof: tan θ = h/a and tan(90° − θ) = cot θ = h/b → (h/a)(h/b) = 1.

Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal; forgetting to add the observer's height when given (a 1.5 m tall man); and mixing up which distance is horizontal. Rationalise answers like 30/√3 to 10√3 to match the options.

When a man of height 1.8 m sees a tower top at 45° from 30 m away, the tower height is 30 + 1.8 = 31.8 m, not 30 m.
Heights and distances summary.
points: Slant length → use sin or cos
Complementary elevations at a, b → h = √(ab)

cards.title: Angles at a point and on a line
cards.body: Angles at a point add to **360°**; angles on a straight line (linear pair) add to **180°**; **vertically opposite angles** are equal.

cards.title: Parallel lines
cards.body: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines: **corresponding angles** are equal, **alternate interior angles** are equal, and **co-interior angles** (same side) add to 180°. The converses prove lines parallel.

cards.title: Triangle facts
points: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles
Sum of any two sides > third side
Larger side is opposite the larger angle

cards.title: Congruence rules
points: Not valid: SSA (in general) and AAA
Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT)

cards.title: Similarity
points: AA, SSS (proportional), SAS (one angle, sides about it proportional)
Ratio of areas = square of ratio of sides
Basic proportionality (Thales): a line parallel to one side divides the other two proportionally

cards.title: Concurrency
cards.body: **Medians** meet at the centroid (divides each median 2 : 1); **altitudes** meet at the orthocentre; angle bisectors at the incentre; perpendicular bisectors at the circumcentre.

cards.title: Pythagoras and triples
cards.body: In a right triangle, hyp² = sum of squares of other sides. Triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29.

cards.q: Two similar triangles have sides in ratio 2 : 3. Their areas are in ratio:
An exterior angle of a triangle is 110° and one interior opposite angle is 45°. The other interior opposite angle is:
Which is NOT a congruence criterion?
cards.explain: AAA gives similar, not necessarily congruent, triangles.

notes.p:
The CDS geometry syllabus lists theorems on **angles at a point**, **parallel lines**, **sides and angles of a triangle**, **congruency**, **similar triangles**, **concurrence of medians and altitudes**, quadrilaterals, circles and loci.

Complementary angles sum to 90°, supplementary to 180°. When two lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal and adjacent ones are supplementary.

**Example 1.** Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal; one co-interior angle is (3x + 10)° and the other (2x + 20)°. Find x.
Step 1: Co-interior angles sum to 180°: 5x + 30 = 180.
Step 2: **x = 30**; the angles are 100° and 80°.

notes.h: Sides and angles of a triangle
notes.p:
The angle sum is 180°; the exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. The **triangle inequality** (sum of two sides > third) decides whether three lengths can form a triangle: 3, 4, 8 cannot (3 + 4 < 8).

The longest side is opposite the largest angle. In an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal; in an equilateral one each angle is 60°.

Two triangles are **congruent** if they match exactly. Valid tests: **SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS** (right angle, hypotenuse, side). After proving congruence, use **CPCT** to conclude other sides or angles are equal. This is how one proves that the perpendicular from the apex of an isosceles triangle bisects the base.

Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides. **Basic proportionality theorem:** if DE ∥ BC in triangle ABC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.

**Example 2.** In triangle ABC, DE ∥ BC with AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm and BC = 15 cm. Find DE and the ratio of areas of ADE to ABC.
Step 1: Triangles ADE and ABC are similar with ratio AD/AB = 4/10 = 2/5.
Step 2: DE = (2/5) × 15 = **6 cm**.
Step 3: Area ratio = (2/5)² = **4 : 25**.

The **angle bisector theorem**: the bisector of angle A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC.

The three medians meet at the **centroid G**, which divides each median in the ratio **2 : 1** from the vertex, and the medians divide the triangle into six triangles of equal area. The altitudes meet at the **orthocentre**; in a right triangle it is the vertex of the right angle, and in an obtuse triangle it lies outside. In an equilateral triangle the centroid, orthocentre, incentre and circumcentre coincide.

**Example 3.** A median is 12 cm. Distance from vertex to centroid = 2/3 × 12 = **8 cm**.
Triangle geometry.
points: Parallel lines: corresponding, alternate equal; co-interior 180°
Exterior angle = sum of opposite interior angles
Congruence: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS

cards.title: Parallelogram properties
points: Opposite angles equal; adjacent angles sum to 180°
A diagonal divides it into two congruent triangles

cards.title: Special parallelograms
points: Rhombus: all sides equal, diagonals perpendicular bisectors
Square: rectangle + rhombus; diagonals equal and perpendicular

cards.title: Mid-point theorem
cards.body: The segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is **parallel to the third side and half of it**. Joining the mid-points of any quadrilateral's sides always gives a parallelogram.

cards.title: Locus
cards.body: A **locus** is the set of all points satisfying a condition. Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the **perpendicular bisector**; points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the **angle bisectors**; points at fixed distance r from a point form a **circle**.

cards.title: Rhombus side
cards.body: Diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Half-diagonals 8 and 6 meet at 90°, so side = √(64 + 36) = **10 cm**.

cards.title: Area facts
cards.body: Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have **equal area**. A triangle on the same base and between the same parallels has **half** that area.

cards.q: In a parallelogram, one angle is 70°. The adjacent angle is:
The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B is:
options: a circle through A and B
cards.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from A and B.

cards.q: Diagonal of a square is 10√2 cm. Its area is:

notes.p:
A **parallelogram** has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. The syllabus asks for properties of **angles, sides and diagonals** of a parallelogram, rectangle and square. Each property has a converse that proves a quadrilateral is a parallelogram: if the diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, it is a parallelogram.

**Example 1.** In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = (2x + 10)° and ∠C = (3x − 20)°. Find all angles.
Step 1: Opposite angles are equal: 2x + 10 = 3x − 20 → x = 30.
Step 2: ∠A = ∠C = 70°, so ∠B = ∠D = **110°**.
points: Sum of angles of a quadrilateral = 360°
A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides
A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides

notes.p:
A **rectangle** is a parallelogram with a right angle; its diagonals are equal. A **rhombus** is a parallelogram with equal sides; its diagonals bisect each other at right angles and bisect the vertex angles. A **square** has all these properties.

**Example 2.** A rectangle has sides 8 cm and 6 cm. Diagonal = √(64 + 36) = **10 cm**, and the diagonals bisect each other into 5 cm halves.

Sum of squares of the sides of a parallelogram = sum of squares of its diagonals (2a² + 2b² = d₁² + d₂²).

**Example 3.** P, Q, R are mid-points of sides of a triangle with sides 8, 10, 12 cm. Perimeter of PQR?
Step 1: Each side of PQR is half a side of the original.
Step 2: Perimeter = (8 + 10 + 12)/2 = **15 cm**; its area is one-quarter of the original.

Triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have equal areas — a fact used in many "show that areas are equal" problems.

The syllabus ends geometry with **loci**. Standard loci:
• Fixed distance from a point → circle.
• Fixed distance from a line → two parallel lines.
• Equidistant from two points → perpendicular bisector of the joining segment.
• Equidistant from two intersecting lines → the pair of angle bisectors.
• Vertex of a right angle on a fixed hypotenuse AB → circle with AB as diameter.

The **circumcentre** is where perpendicular-bisector loci meet (equidistant from all three vertices); the **incentre** is where angle-bisector loci meet (equidistant from all three sides).

Assuming a rectangle's diagonals are perpendicular (only in a square), or a rhombus's diagonals are equal (only in a square). In locus questions, "equidistant from two lines" has two bisectors, not one.
Quadrilaterals and loci.
points: Rectangle: equal diagonals; rhombus: perpendicular diagonals
Mid-point segment ∥ third side, half its length
Equidistant from two points → perpendicular bisector
Fixed distance from a point → circle

cards.title: Chord properties
points: Perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre
Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference on the same arc
Angles in the same segment are equal

cards.title: Cyclic quadrilateral
cards.body: A quadrilateral with all four vertices on a circle. **Opposite angles add to 180°**, and an exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.

cards.title: Tangents
points: Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact
Two tangents from an external point are equal
Alternate segment: angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment

cards.title: Normal
cards.body: The **normal** at a point of a circle is the line perpendicular to the tangent there; for a circle it always passes through the **centre** (it lies along the radius).

cards.title: Chord length
cards.body: A chord is 3 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Half-chord = √(25 − 9) = 4, so chord = **8 cm**.

cards.title: Intersecting chords and secants
points: Chords AB, CD meeting at P inside: PA·PB = PC·PD
Tangent PT and secant PAB from outside: PT² = PA·PB

cards.title: Common tangents
cards.body: Two circles: direct common tangent length = √(d² − (r₁ − r₂)²); transverse = √(d² − (r₁ + r₂)²).

cards.q: An angle subtended by an arc at the centre is 100°. The angle subtended at the remaining circumference is:
From a point 13 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm, the tangent length is:
In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 75°. ∠C is:
cards.explain: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

notes.p:
The syllabus mentions **circles and their properties, including tangents and normals**. Start with chords: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord **bisects** it, so every chord question becomes a right triangle with the radius as hypotenuse.

**Example 1.** Two parallel chords of lengths 16 cm and 30 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre of a circle of radius 17 cm. Distance between them?
Step 1: Distance of 16 cm chord: √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15.
Step 2: Distance of 30 cm chord: √(17² − 15²) = √64 = 8.
Step 3: Opposite sides → 15 + 8 = **23 cm** (same side would be 7 cm).
points: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre
The longest chord is the diameter
Only one circle passes through three non-collinear points

notes.p:
The angle an arc subtends at the **centre is twice** the angle at any point on the remaining circle. Consequences: angles in the same segment are equal, and the **angle in a semicircle is 90°**.

In a **cyclic quadrilateral**, opposite angles are supplementary. **Example 2.** ABCD is cyclic with ∠ABC = 92° and ∠BAD = 64°. Then ∠ADC = 180 − 92 = **88°** and ∠BCD = 180 − 64 = **116°**.

A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is **perpendicular to the radius** there; the normal at that point is the radius line itself. Tangents from an external point are equal in length and make equal angles with the line joining the point to the centre.

**Example 3.** A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle, with AB = 6, BC = 7, CD = 4. Find AD.
Step 1: Equal tangent lengths give AB + CD = BC + AD.
Step 2: 6 + 4 = 7 + AD → **AD = 3**.

**Example 4.** Two tangents from P make an angle of 60°. The angle at the centre between the radii to the points of contact is 180 − 60 = **120°**.

notes.h: Alternate segment and power of a point
notes.p:
The angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the **alternate segment**. From an external point P, **PT² = PA × PB** for a tangent PT and secant PAB. Inside the circle, intersecting chords satisfy PA × PB = PC × PD.

If PA = 4 and PB = 9 on a secant, the tangent from P is √36 = **6**.

Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference; adding instead of subtracting chord distances when chords are on the same side; and applying cyclic-quadrilateral results to quadrilaterals that are not cyclic.
Circle theorems.
points: Tangent ⟂ radius; normal passes through centre
Tangents from a point are equal
Tangential quadrilateral: AB + CD = BC + AD

chapters.title: Maths: areas of plane figures & field book

cards.title: Area formulas
points: Trapezium = ½(sum of parallel sides) × height

cards.title: Field book
cards.body: A **field book** records a surveyor's measurements: distances along a base line (the chain line) and **offsets** — perpendicular distances to boundary corners on either side. The plot then splits into right triangles and trapeziums whose areas are added.

cards.title: Path around a lawn
cards.body: Lawn 40 m × 30 m with a 2 m path outside. Outer: 44 × 34 = 1,496. Path = 1,496 − 1,200 = **296 m²**.

cards.title: Scaling
cards.body: If every length is multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k². Radius up 10% → area up 21%.

cards.q: Area of an equilateral triangle with side 6 cm:
A wheel of radius 35 cm makes 100 revolutions. Distance covered (π = 22/7):
Area of a trapezium with parallel sides 10 cm and 14 cm and height 5 cm:

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus lists **areas of squares, rectangles, parallelograms, triangles and circles**, and of **figures that can be split into these (field book)**.

Use the formula that fits the given data: for a triangle with base and height use ½bh; with three sides use **Heron's formula**; with two sides and the included angle use ½ab sin C; for an equilateral triangle use (√3/4)a², with height (√3/2)a.
points: π = 22/7 or 3.14 as the question says

notes.p:
Break the figure into known shapes, then add or subtract.

**Example 1.** A square of side 14 cm has four quadrants of radius 7 cm cut from its corners. Remaining area?
Step 1: Square = 196 cm².
Step 2: Four quadrants = one full circle of radius 7 = 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm².
Step 3: Remaining = **42 cm²**.

**Example 2.** Area of a ring between circles of radii 10 cm and 4 cm = π(100 − 16) = 84π ≈ **263.9 cm²** (π = 3.1416).

In a field book, the chain line runs up the middle of the page with distances from the start; offsets to the left and right are written beside it. Each pair of consecutive offsets on the same side forms a **trapezium** (or a triangle at the ends).

**Example 3.** A chain line AD = 100 m. Offsets on one side: B at 30 m with 20 m offset, C at 70 m with 30 m offset. Area on that side?
Step 1: Triangle A to B: ½ × 30 × 20 = 300.
Step 2: Trapezium B to C: ½ × (20 + 30) × 40 = 1,000.
Step 3: Triangle C to D: ½ × 30 × 30 = 450.
Step 4: Total = **1,750 m²**.
Repeat for the other side and add.

A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the circle. **Example 4.** A minute hand 14 cm long sweeps for 15 minutes (90°). Area swept = ¼ × 22/7 × 196 = **154 cm²**.

Distance covered by a wheel = revolutions × circumference. Number of revolutions = distance ÷ (2πr).

Mixing units (m and cm) — convert first; using diameter in place of radius; and forgetting that a path "inside" a lawn reduces the inner dimensions instead of increasing the outer. In percentage-change questions use the k² scaling rule rather than recalculating.

**Example 5.** The radius of a circle is increased by 20%. Area increase = 1.2² − 1 = 0.44, i.e. **44%** — no need to compute πr² twice. Circumference, being a length, rises by only 20%.
Area formulas.
points: Field book: triangles + trapeziums from offsets

chapters.title: Maths: surface areas & volumes of solids

cards.title: Cuboid and cube
points: Cuboid volume lbh; TSA 2(lb + bh + hl)
Cube volume a³; TSA 6a²; diagonal a√3

cards.title: Cylinder and cone
points: Cylinder: volume πr²h; CSA 2πrh; TSA 2πr(r + h)
Cone: volume ⅓πr²h; slant l = √(r² + h²)
Cone CSA πrl; TSA πr(l + r)

cards.title: Melting and recasting
cards.body: A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into a cylinder of radius 4 cm. (4/3)π(216) = π(16)h → 288 = 16h → **h = 18 cm**.

cards.title: Volume conserved
cards.body: Melting, recasting and pouring keep **volume** constant; surface area changes. Number of small solids = big volume ÷ small volume.

cards.q: Volume of a cube is 512 cm³. Its total surface area is:
If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its volume becomes:
A cylinder and cone have the same base and height. Ratio of their volumes:

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus asks for **surface area and volume of cuboids**, **lateral surface and volume of right circular cones and cylinders**, and **surface area and volume of spheres**. Hemispheres, cubes and combinations of these appear regularly.

Total surface area counts every face; curved (lateral) surface area leaves out the flat ends. Volume is measured in cubic units, and 1 litre = 1,000 cm³; 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.
points: Cube is a cuboid with l = b = h
Cone volume is one-third of the cylinder on the same base and height
Hemisphere TSA includes the flat circle

notes.p:
**Example 1.** A room is 10 m × 8 m × 4 m. Find the area of the four walls and the longest rod that fits.
Step 1: Four walls = 2h(l + b) = 2 × 4 × 18 = **144 m²**.
Step 2: Longest rod = diagonal = √(100 + 64 + 16) = √180 = **6√5 m** ≈ 13.4 m.

If the edge of a cube is increased by 50%, surface area grows by 125% (1.5² = 2.25) and volume by 237.5% (1.5³ = 3.375).

**Example 2.** A cylindrical tank of radius 1.4 m and height 2 m. Capacity in litres?
Step 1: V = 22/7 × 1.96 × 2 = 12.32 m³.
Step 2: × 1,000 = **12,320 litres**.

For a cone, find the slant height first if CSA is needed. A sector of a circle rolled into a cone: sector radius becomes the **slant height**, and arc length becomes the base circumference 2πr.

**Example 3.** How many lead shots of radius 1 cm can be made from a cuboid 11 cm × 10 cm × 8 cm? (π = 22/7)
Step 1: Cuboid volume = 880 cm³.
Step 2: One shot = (4/3) × 22/7 × 1 = 88/21 cm³.
Step 3: Number = 880 × 21/88 = **210**.

For a toy made of a cone on a hemisphere, add the two volumes, and add the cone's CSA to the hemisphere's CSA (not their TSAs — the joined circle is hidden).

Using TSA when CSA is asked (painting the outside of a pipe, a tent with no floor); forgetting the ⅓ for a cone; mixing diameter and radius; and forgetting litre conversions. In recasting problems, never equate surface areas.

**Example 4.** A hollow pipe has outer radius 4 cm, inner radius 3 cm and length 21 cm. Volume of metal = π(R² − r²)h = 22/7 × 7 × 21 = **462 cm³**. Hollow-object questions always use the difference of the two radii squared, not the square of the thickness.
Solid formulas.
points: Cuboid lbh; 2(lb + bh + hl); diagonal √(l² + b² + h²)
Cone ⅓πr²h; CSA πrl; l = √(r² + h²)

chapters.title: Maths: statistics — data, graphs & central tendency

cards.title: Collection and tabulation
cards.body: **Primary data** is collected first-hand; **secondary data** comes from existing sources. Raw data is organised into a **frequency distribution**: classes, tally marks and frequencies. Class mark = (lower + upper limit)/2; class width = upper − lower.

cards.title: Graphs
cards.body: **Bar chart**: separate bars for categories. **Histogram**: adjacent bars for continuous classes, area ∝ frequency. **Frequency polygon**: joins mid-points of histogram tops. **Pie chart**: sector angle = (value/total) × 360°. **Ogive**: cumulative frequency curve, used for the median.

cards.title: Median and mode
points: Median (raw): middle value after ordering; even n → average of two middle
Grouped mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h

cards.title: Quick properties
cards.body: Adding a constant to every value adds it to mean, median and mode. Multiplying every value by k multiplies all three by k. The sum of deviations from the mean is always **0**.

cards.q: Mean of the first 10 natural numbers is:
Median of 7, 3, 9, 4, 12, 6 is:
If mean = 20 and median = 22, the mode by the empirical formula is:

notes.p:
The CDS syllabus covers **collection and tabulation of statistical data**, **graphical representation** (frequency polygons, histograms, bar charts, pie charts) and **measures of central tendency**.

Data is either **ungrouped** (raw list) or **grouped** into classes. In **exclusive** classes (10–20, 20–30) the upper limit belongs to the next class; **inclusive** classes (10–19, 20–29) must be converted to continuous ones (9.5–19.5) before drawing a histogram or applying median and mode formulas.

Choose the graph to match the data. **Bar charts** compare separate categories (bar widths equal, gaps allowed). **Histograms** show continuous classes with no gaps; with unequal class widths, heights must be adjusted so that **area is proportional to frequency**. A **frequency polygon** joins class-mark points and is closed at both ends at the mid-points of empty classes. A **pie chart** shows parts of a whole: sector angle = (component/total) × 360°.

The **less-than ogive** and **more-than ogive** intersect at the **median**.

**Example 1.** Find the mean.
Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 with frequencies 5, 8, 4, 3.
Step 1: Class marks 5, 15, 25, 35.
Step 2: Σfx = 25 + 120 + 100 + 105 = 350; Σf = 20.
Step 3: Mean = 350/20 = **17.5**.

If the mean of n numbers is x̄ and one number is replaced, new mean = x̄ + (new − old)/n. Combined mean of two groups = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂).

**Example 2.** Using the same table, find the median.
Step 1: N = 20, N/2 = 10. Cumulative frequencies: 5, 13, 17, 20.
Step 2: The 10th value lies in 10–20 (cf jumps from 5 to 13). l = 10, cf = 5, f = 8, h = 10.
Step 3: Median = 10 + [(10 − 5)/8] × 10 = 10 + 6.25 = **16.25**.

**Mode** for grouped data uses the modal class (highest frequency): here 10–20 with f₁ = 8, f₀ = 5, f₂ = 4. Mode = 10 + [(8 − 5)/(16 − 5 − 4)] × 10 = 10 + 30/7 ≈ **14.29**.

For ungrouped data, the mode is the most frequent value; a set can have more than one mode.

Using class limits instead of class marks for the mean; forgetting to order data before finding the median; drawing a histogram with gaps; and in pie charts forgetting that percentages × 3.6 gives degrees (25% → 90°). The median formula needs the cumulative frequency of the class **before** the median class.
Statistics formulas.
